blog_personal_01_luna.text:
How We Potty Trained Our Toddler in 10 Days (And Three Big Abject Failures First)

Our daughter Maya is 2 years 9 months on May 14. We were really ready for this in June. Sticker charts—she never even looked at it. Let her run around naked—three puddles on the rug. We used this ‘gentle’ weekend process—so much prompting, she would hide behind the couch when we said the word toilet.

Enter: long weekend home in Sacramento June 7-16. Rather than approaching potty training like a test, we needed to approach it like a process to be learned.

Day 1: No diapers during the day. Got 6 cheap pairs of cotton underwear (bought these) and let Maya pick the purple ones. Got little floor potty in the bathroom (waterproof pad under it too). Every 45 minutes, we quietly said ‘It’s potty time.’ (We weren’t asking ‘do you need to go?’) If she wouldn’t do it, we didn’t fight. We would just try again.

Most important: we made it her. We would have her bring her underwear to the laundry basket. She would flush the toilet. We let her have one little treat from the treasure box after every successful use (usually temporary tattoo or plastic animal under $2). When there was an accident, it was boring. 'Pee goes in the potty. Let’s clean up.' No shame, no talking about it.

Day 3 and 4 were very hard. Monday had six accidents. I almost gave up (one of the accidents was in the library in East Sacramento). But our pediatrician had told us there would be ups and downs in the first week, so we just kept going.

By Day 6, she could go two hours sometimes. Day 8 she said ‘I have to poop’ and made it to the potty just in time. It felt like we won the marathon.

We used diapers for nap and night, because nighttime dryness is its own developmental thing. By Day 10 she was regular at potty in the day (even when we went to the grocery store, McKinley Park).

We didn’t use a perfect process. We just used consistency and less words and reasonable expectations and made it her.

blog_personal_03_glm.text:
Grading papers instead of billing: My first semester as a teacher 
 In August 2023, I left Hendricks & Cole after 14 years as a corporate attorney and went to Room 214 at Roosevelt High School with a provisional teaching license and lots of fear. I was 42 and it was the first birthday I didn't check email on my phone in 10 years. 
 Why did I leave? I defended a merger in 2022 that put 300 people out of work in a town of 8000 and I couldn't stop thinking about it. My sister (who has taught 4th grade in Duluth for 20 years) said something that resonated: "You're always trying to figure out what things cost. You should try figuring out what things are worth." 
 Here is my first semester of teaching 11th grade civics and 1 (yes, our district does) section of constitutional law. 
 I get paid $52,400/year. I made that by March in 2019. But I've never once had dinner at my desk. And I stopped taking migraine meds in November because (knock on wood) I no longer need to. 
 I'm humbled by the learning curve. I went to Yale Law and Big Law for 12 years. I really thought managing a classroom would just be "leadership skills." Well, it's not. It wasn't until late September that I realized my 3rd period class (31 sophomores) would only be quiet if I let Marcus have "news of the day" as his intro. Now it's the highlight of my morning. 
 The worst week was Oct 16th. I worked late to do parent-teacher conferences and 6 parents (some suspiciously) asked why a lawyer would want *their kids*. I said honestly: because a girl in 2nd period civics (Priya) asked me if the 1st Amendment protects her TikTok. Best question anyone has asked me in years. 
 Final exams wrapped Dec 20th. When I closed the gradebook, 84% of my students passed. And one kid (Diego) told me he wants to be a lawyer now. I didn't cry but it was close. 
 My bar card is still in my wallet. Old habits die hard. But at 7:45 AM tomorrow when the bell rings, I know where I'd rather be.

blog_personal_05_sonnet.text:
Flew into Kansai on a Tuesday in October, top of my budget was ¥15,000/day (about $100), and it left me sure that Kyoto is one of the easiest cities to do it in, just switch out taxis for a bike and Michelin for tofu. 
 Day one: Haikyu Hostel near Kyoto Station, ¥3400/night dorm bed. Get ICOCA card at kiosk in station. 
 Rent bike at hostel (¥800/day), no buses needed (Kyoto is flat, bike lanes all over), ¥450 pastry+coffee from Lawson konbini (breakfast), 
 Take bike to Fushimi Inari before 8am (before tour buses) - the gates are free to enter, 40min walk to Yotsutsuji overlook 
 Standing soba place near shrine, lunch, ¥600 for kitsune soba. 
 Spend afternoon at Tofuku-ji, ¥500 entry to get in for the garden, then bike to Gion and just walk around. Free to walk Hanamikoji St, free to peek in Yasaka Shrine. 
 Bowl of ramen at counter place in Pontocho, dinner, ¥900. 
 Buy can of Asahi from vending machine, ¥150. 
 Total for day one is about ¥10,200. Under budget. 
 Day two: Skip hostel breakfast, get onigiri from konbini, ¥300 
 Bike to Arashiyama, bamboo grove, free, best before 9am (before crowds - just you and the rustle of the stalks) 
 Next door, Tenryu-ji temple - ¥500 entry for pond garden, worth it 
 Walk across Togetsukyo Bridge. 
 Curry cheap lunch near station, ¥750 
 Early afternoon in Nishiki Market - grazing not eating full meal. Get skewer here, bite of tamagoyaki there, spend maybe ¥1200 total enough to call it lunch+snack 
 Go to Kiyomizu-dera in late afternoon light, ¥400 entry 
 Walk down through Sannenzaka+Ninenzaka - free but the nicest streets 
 Last dinner: katsu curry ¥1,100 
 Total for two days/two nights about ¥19,000. So I already saved enough for almost a full day more in my budget on day two. 
 Just avoid deprivation - go to temples before the crowd (and before you get the urge to spend stupid money on tea to avoid the crowd) and make your bike half your transport budget.

Flew in to Kansai on a Tuesday in October, budgeted ¥15k ($100) a day and left thinking Kyoto is a fairly easy city to pull off - you're basically just swapping cabs for a bike and Michelin-star restaurants for tofu houses. 
 Day 1: arrived Haikyu Hostel near Kyoto Station, ¥3400 a night for dorm bed. Got an ICOCA card at station kiosk. Used hostel rental bike ¥800/day rather than bus - Kyoto is very flat and full of bike paths. Breakfast was coffee and bun at Lawson konbini, ¥450. Bicycled to Fushimi Inari before 8am - beat the tour buses. Free entry to the gates and you can hike to Yotsutsuji overlook point in ~40 min. Lunch at standing soba house close to the shrine - ¥600 for kitsune soba. Afternoon at Tofuku-ji temple (entry ¥500) for garden. Bicycled to Gion and walked around. Free to walk through Hanamikoji and check out Yasaka Shrine (free). Dinner: bowl of ramen at ramen counter in Pontocho, ¥900. And a can of Asahi from the vending machine, ¥150. So day 1 total: ¥10,200-ish, still under budget. 
 Day 2: hostel no-breakfast so breakfast onigiri from konbini, ¥300. Bicycled to Arashiyama for bamboo grove (free). Best time before 9am - just you and the sound of the bamboo creaking. Adjacent Tenryu-ji temple is ¥500 and nice pond garden. Walk over Togetsukyo Bridge. Cheap curry lunch near station, ¥750. Mid afternoon explore Nishiki Market - just graze instead of sit down meal. Skewer here, tamagoyaki there. ¥1200-ish spent for enough food to pass as lunch/snack. Hit Kiyomizu-dera in the afternoon - nice light. Entry ¥400. Walked back down the Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka - free but most beautiful streets in town. Final dinner: katsu curry, ¥1100. 
 End of 2 days, 2 nights, ¥19,000-ish total. And I'd saved ~entire extra day's budget as of day 2. So basically not about living like a monk, it's about seeing the temples early (before the crowds & before you want to avoid the crowds with overpriced tea purchases) and using bike to sub half of your transportation costs.

blog_personal_07_luna.text:
On January 1, 2025, I removed Facebook and Instagram from my phone. My plan was to go without them for 6 months. There was no grand announcement. I just told my close friends and family to text me instead.

The initial break was oddly physical. I’d grab my phone waiting for coffee at Blue Bottle in Oakland. Instinctively reach for Instagram. And suddenly realize it was gone. The first week I probably checked my phone 30 times a day for no real reason. By February, much less so. I carried a paperback with me instead. Mostly novels. But I also cracked open a gardening book that’d been on my nightstand since 2023 (unopened since 2023!).

The most striking effect was how much calmer my brain felt. I hadn’t realized how much I was comparing my regular Tuesday to someone’s polished vacation, kitchen remodel, or professional break-through. Without all that input, I wasn’t feeling so slightly out of step with my life. And I found I retained more of what I read and heard. Rather than pre-sleep browsing, I read with my daughter, Maya, for 20 minutes. We made it through five chapter books in January-June.

I thought I’d be cut off from important news and friends. A few birthdays were missed. Some friendships I realized were largely upheld by likes and story replies. But I also talked more. I called my college friend, Daniel, in Chicago twice. We hadn’t done that in years. My sister and I started exchanging Sunday voice notes.

Going back was the tough part. I re-installed Facebook and Instagram on July 1. I thought I’d be fresh and virtuous. But within 3 days, I was right back in old habits. I deleted them again. I’m now only using Facebook on my laptop for some family groups.

Six months away from the social feeds didn’t make me a better, more enlightened me. But it did help me become aware of my choices (and the choices made for me). I realized that actually, I don’t miss the social media stuff too much. I miss some people. And I now know to reach out to them.

blog_personal_09_glm.text:
Baking Sourdough at 5,000 Feet: Learning From 30 Failed Loaves

Last June, we moved from Chicago to Boulder. I thought I'd be able to carry my sourdough know-how with me. I'd been making incredible loaves at sea level for two years, my sourdough starter ("Gerald," named after my grandfather) was on fire. Then I baked my first loaf here (5,430 feet altitude) and emerged with the worst hockey puck a brick could ever wish to be—tasting like disappointment.

First eight loaves: sticky, dense centers. Loaves 9-15: brown on bottom, raw in the middle. By the time we reached loaf 20, Dave was nudging me toward buying bread. No way! I was too far gone.

Here's something they don't tell you when you bake in high altitudes: water has a lower boiling point (202°F vs. 212°F at sea level). Air pressure is about 17% less. Bread dough rises fast, then collapses just as fast. Because I had my 4-hour bulk ferment routine from sea level, the dough was over-proofing too quickly. It couldn't support itself.

Loaf 30 brought me to the phone begging Marta the baker at Denver's Flour Bakery for advice. She (kindly) laughed and gave me the following advice that worked:

(1) Reduce water by around 8%. (From 350g to 322g water for 500g flour). Dough needs more structure in higher altitudes. Period. (2) Go from 4 hours bulk ferment to 2.5. Stop timing anything. Wait for a 50% rise now instead of doubling. (3) This was almost blasphemous, but now I started using 75g vs. 100g starter to slow it all down.

When I baked, I increased my Dutch oven temp from 475°F to 500°F for first 20 minutes (with cover). Then, down to 450°F (uncovered) for 22 minutes instead of 25. This quicker initial bake time helped the crust form before the middle over-expanded and caved.

Loaf 31 (a snowy Saturday last January) looked like I could have hung a picture off it. Ears were superb. Crumb was shiny, open, and slightly tangy. My kids (Mia 7 & Owen 4) who have graciously put up with my failures have clapped.

It wasn't about adjusting the hydration percentage, though. It was about unlearning. I had to unlearn two years of "I know what I'm doing" before I could adjust. Gerald and I are back to being learners. Not such a bad thing.

If you're baking over 4,000 feet and having trouble. It's not your starter. It's not you. Adjust. Pay more attention to the dough than time. Keep going past loaf 30.

Baking at 5000 Feet (and How 30 Disasters Helped Me)

Moving from Chicago to Boulder last June, I thought I’d bring my sourdough prowess with me. My sourdough starter, named “Gerald” after my grandfather, was making beautiful bread for 2 years in the flatlands. Then, my first loaf at 5,430 feet produced a hockey puck the consistency of a brick with a side of despair.

Bread 1 - 8: Solid center, gummy consistency. Bread 9 - 15: Soot on the bottom, uncooked middle. By bread 20, my husband Dave was gently asking if maybe we should just go buy some bread. No way, I said. I’d come too far.

What no one tells you about baking at altitude. Water temperature is lower. (We’re at 202°F. At sea level it’s 212°F) Pressure is about 17% lower. Dough over-proofs and collapses quickly, but looks to rise easily at first. My standard 4hr. bulk ferment at sea level was causing over-proofing before I knew it. Couldn't hold structure.

By bread 30 I found myself on the phone begging a woman at Flour Bakery in Denver named Marta for help. (Marta was nice about it. She laughed.) This is what changed the game.

1) I reduced the water by about 8%. (350g to 322g water for 500g of flour.) High altitude dough needs more structure.

2) I lowered bulk ferment time from 4hr to 2.5hr. I've stopped paying attention to time entirely. Now, I look for 50% rise, rather than double.

3) It seemed blasphemous, but... I went from 100g starter to 75g to slow things down.

To bake, I went from 475°F to 500°F in my Dutch Oven for the first 20 minutes, with the lid on, then to 450°F w/o lid for 22 minutes, rather than 25. The high heat gets the crust going before it can over-expand and collapse on the inside.

Bread 31, baked one snowy Saturday this past January, had an ear that could hold a picture frame. A nice open crumb. Glossy. Slightly sour. My kids, Mia (7) and Owen (4) - who had been very patient with my bread disasters - were cheering.

It wasn't a matter of hydration. It was about letting go. I had to let go of 2 years of "I know what I'm doing" to learn how to adjust. Gerald and I are learners again. And you know what? That's not a bad place to be.

If you're over 4000 feet and having difficulty with your bread: your sourdough starter's not broken and neither are you. Adjust, pay attention to the dough instead of the time, and keep going past bread 30.

blog_personal_11_sonnet.text:
On October 14th of last year, I pressed send on my first invoice for $340 to write a blog post on industrial water filtration (something I knew nothing about 3 days before). And now I've sent 118 more. $38,240 so far this year. 27 clients. Here's the story of what really happened before I package it up nicely.

I wasn't surprised by the total but I was by the breakdown. $24,000 goes to 4 clients:

Ledgerly, a SaaS company, gives me $1,400/mo to write a newsletter and 2 blogs. Ohio dental marketing agency sends me $600/week every week like clockwork. All the other 23 (one-offs for landing pages, email sequences, $75 for a product description on a dog leash company etc) amounted to $14k and probably ate up 60% of my time. I didn't realize the difference between fixed costs and retainers until I made a graph in July.

1. I charged a one-time rate of $2,200 for "website copy" to a fintech client without clarifying pages. 11 pages in March and effectively I was at $9/hr. I finished because I said I would.

2. I didn't save up for taxes until my accountant (Priya) asked if I did estimated payments in April. No, I didn't. $6100 to pay by June 15th. Had to borrow from savings.

3. I put up with a client (supplement brand) for 5 months after I started getting payments 20-30 days late. Because I liked it. When I finally dropped the client in August they owed me $1900. (I never got it all).

Doesn't mean it wasn't worth it. I quit a $61k/salary job in September of last year so $38240 from scratch learning all of the above in a year isn't bad. Year 2. Less clients. Better contracts. A way to cut out late payers at 15 days instead of 5 months (kill switch).

January 2025. My A1C was 8.4%. Sick of the silliness of 'well, I'm eating pretty good'. My doctor, Dr. Lena Morales at Kaiser Permanente in Sacramento, suggested I take meds. No, I'm not having any serious symptoms so let's try six months of logging, food, walking, sleep, weight loss etc.

I bought an inexpensive spiral notebook. Food, time, portions, how I felt. First breakfast: '7:30 am- Bagel with cream cheese. Banana. Coffee'. Two hours later, my glucose read: 196 mg/dL. Not a panic, but a pattern. Toast, rice, cereal, too much potato, got my number up fast.

So by February, I'm doing eggs with spinach. Plain Greek yogurt with walnuts. Left over chicken and veggies. Still do Taco Friday at El Rincon on Fruitridge Rd. but now two not four. No horchata or sugary stuff. Dinner time walk in my neighborhood with my wife, Marisol. Twenty minutes. But then it's 35 minutes. Five nights a week.

It's not about the perfect. It's about being consistent. April. My grandson Mateo's birthday. I had a piece of chocolate cake. Logged it. No, I didn't blow it. Journaling gave me insight. It wasn't the piece of cake that was an issue. It was going off the rails for three weeks.

My June appointment. A1C down to 7.1%. September, down to 6.5%. Lost 24 pounds since January. And January 10, 2026. Last test: 6.1%. No diabetes meds this year. But with frequent visits and ok from my doctor. I still test. I know things may change.

Now I've got these notebooks stacked next to my coffee maker. Days were not all perfect, but there's evidence, there, that taking small steps -- eat less rice, eat more veggies, walk after dinner -- can lead to an entirely different year.

I picked up a dollar-store spiral-bound notebook and began logging everything—not just what I was eating, but when, how much, and how I felt. My very first breakfast entry? "7:30 a.m. - Bagel and cream cheese, banana, coffee." And two hours later, my glucose was 196 mg/dL. I didn't freak out, but I did notice a trend. Toast, rice, cereal and huge plates of potatoes were skyrocketing my readings.

Come February I was eating eggs with spinach, plain Greek yogurt with walnuts or leftovers like chicken and veggies. Tacos on Friday at El Rincon on Fruitridge road, sure, but two, not four. No sweet horchata. My wife (Marisol) and I walked around our neighborhood after dinner—for 20 minutes. Those little strolls grew into 35-minute walks five days a week.

The key wasn't perfection—it was consistency. When my grandson Mateo's birthday came in April, I had a piece of chocolate cake. I logged it. I didn't write off the day. My journal showed me it wasn't the one slice; it was the fact I quit for three weeks after that.

By my next checkup (June), my A1C dropped to 7.1%. Come September, I was at 6.5%. I'd lost 24 lbs since January. My last check, Jan 10 2026, it was 6.1%. So, this year I haven't needed to take meds for diabetes, but that's only because I've kept up with regular visits and my doctor has been okay with it. I still check my glucose. I'm prepared to pivot if needed.

Now, my stack of notebooks sits next to the coffee machine. I've got some bad days in there, sure, but I also have evidence that even small choices—less rice, more veggies, a post-dinner walk—can make for an entirely new year.

On March 8, 2023, I cracked my laptop open at 7:45am PT before even brewing my morning coffee. Email was first thing. No Meta access. 11 years in tech. 4 years as a technical program manager on Reality Labs. Gone. Left with a calendar invite titled 'Important Update' that I couldn't make. 
 90 days later, typing from a coffee shop in Austin after just accepting a new role. Here's the recovery strategy that kept me sane. 
 1-14 days: Cry it out. Take two full weeks to wallow. Settled severance (16 weeks + feb bonus prorated - ran all numbers first weekend so i wouldn't freak out later) Uninstalled Slack on phone. DMed ex colleagues victory posts to ignore. Walked Lady Bird lake loop every morning at same time i would've logged on. You need the scaffolding. 
 15-45 days: Lay down your scaffolding. Changed my LinkedIn 3/20. Expected the pity. Instead got notifications exploding. 11 ex colleagues dmed me in a week. 6 of those ex colleagues also let go. Started a 'Laid Off and Loaded on Caffeine' discord. Met virtually every Tuesday. Got referrals from discord - not cold apps. 
 Applied to exactly 40 jobs. End of story. More focus on quality. Every single one got customized resume. Was hunting for warm intro for 30 of them. 
 46-90 days: Practice interviewing like you live on it (you do) 2 mock interviews per week. 1 with my friend Priya. 1 video recorded with loom so I could cringe at my ums and ahs. tanked a sys design at a fintech in April. Let myself sulk for an evening. Drove three pages of notes of what went wrong. 
 Accepted the offer for a program management role at a healthcare startup yesterday. 15% lower base than Meta. But has equity that may or may not be meaningful. Feels better for sleep. My old team had project constant reorg. This company has a road map that hasn't pivoted since January. 
 If you got that calendar invite in March: Here's my entire strategy: Budget your cries. Limit your apps. Lean on your network when your legs fail. 
 90 days. You can survive. You're more than a badge access.

I got notification after notification. 11 of my past co-workers reached out within a week. 6 of them got laid off too. We formed a discord ("Laid Off and Loaded on Caffeine"). We would get together every Tuesday virtually. I got referrals off that. Not from cold applications. 
 I submitted 40 job applications total. That's it. Quality not quantity. Each had a custom resume. I tried to get a warm intro for 30 of them. 
 Days 46-90: Interview like your life depends on it. Because it does. I did two mock interviews a week. One with my friend Priya. One I recorded on Loom to laugh at myself for my filler words. I fumbled a system design question at a fintech company in April. I wallowed for a night. Then I made 3 pages of notes on why I sucked. 
 The offer I just accepted yesterday is for a program manager role at a healthcare startup. 15% lower base than Meta. But equity that might actually be something. I'm sleeping better. My old team had projects that were always getting re-orged. This company has a roadmap that hasn't been changed since January. 
 If you got that "Important Update" calendar invite in March, here's the summary of my plan in one sentence. Grieve in a controlled way. Be judicious with applications. Lean on your network when your legs fail you. 
 You can make it. 90 days. It's not that long. You're not just a badge access level.

essay_opinion_00_glm.text:
I started on Instagram in October 2013. You could only post squares. I cared about filters. Clarendon usually.

Yesterday, March, Tuesday. I deleted it. After 11 years, after like 14k posts and stories and likes.

It didn’t come in some public blow-up — no scandal, no data breach, no rallying cry. It was actually dumbly mundane that I finally called it quits. I realized, like, mid-viewing a reel of some random person in Portugal fixing up a camper van, while my 6 year old was describing the picture she had drawn for me. And I said uh-huh 4 times in a row and like... nothing sunk in. She was just like, uh-huh. And she stopped. Well. That's way worse than a screen time report.

Before this? I tried things. Gray scale. App time limits. Minimalism. All that. But it wasn’t like, the time on Instagram was bad. Though it was like 2+ hours a day on my iphone screen time. It was just Instagram as a locus of attention. Instagram is how I eat. Or watch the sunset. Or look at my flowers. I pre-Instagram things. Like pasta on my aunt’s table in Yonkers. Once rearranged so I’d get better light for it. She still mentions that.

And the most startling thing is, it’s not an addiction thing really. It’s a thing of, like, I’m bored so I go here. Or it’s a tipping point thing. Like, I wake up. So then I do this. I'm waiting for coffee. So then I do this. I’m in line at the bodega.

So I changed the times instead. I put my kindle in my pocket instead of my phone. (9 books since March. That's up from 3 last year.) And a notebook of paper to write in instead of checking stuff when I'm in the bathroom line. Or like I walked to the subway. I walked to it like a dick. Slowly. Not staring at my phone while waiting there.

I won’t say it’s perfect. There were 3 horrible days of phantom thumb swiping for the app that isn’t there anymore on the home screen. I don’t know what half of my acquaintances are doing now sometimes. That sucks a bit. I missed a friend’s engagement announcement. Had to talk.

But here’s something: I am bored again. Really bored. The good kind of boredom that is like, oh, you know that chair wobbles? I’ve meant to fix it for 2 years. So I fixed it. And then I sat down. And I didn’t take a picture for anyone.

If you’re thinking of it, you don’t need a better reason than you want to pay attention to you. I waited for 11 years for a good enough reason to quit. Turns out I can quit because I just wanted to.

I signed up in October 2013, when you could only post square photos, my only worry was the filter. Clarendon, mostly. Then in March, last month, on a Tuesday, I deleted Instagram after 11 years, and about 14,000 posts, stories, and likes.

It wasn’t a big thing. No scandal. No 数据 breach. No I’m-quitting-society-and-all-its-empty-pursuits manifesto. It was embarrassing, actually. The last straw was seeing a reel of some guy doing up a camper in Portugal, while my 6-yr old gave commentary on the drawing she’d just done for me, and I was saying ‘uh-huh’ 4 times and not listening to a single word. She trailed off mid-sentence. That was worse than any screen-time readout.

I’d tried to manage it before. Gray-scale. App time limits. The whole hipster digital-minimalism thing. The time I spent (not that it was 2+ hrs a day, as my iPhone’s screen-time stats showed — but it was no insignificant amount). It was less about the time than it was about how I shaped my attention. Everything was a potential content. Meals. Sunsets. My own yard. I once re-set a plate of pasta at my aunt’s house in Yonkers to get the best lighting. She still mentions it.

The most surprising part was what this behavior actually consisted of. It wasn’t about desire. It was about idle hands and threshold experiences. Waking up. Awaiting coffee. In line at the bodega. So I started filling the gaps differently. Kindle on me instead of phone (9 books since March, only 3 last year). Note paper to take care of the instinct to consult something, anything, in line at the can. Go walk, bad and slow, toward the train instead of in line.

I don’t want to imply everything changed. There were 3 yucky days of phantom thumb swipes on the home screen where the app used to be. I’m still not really sure what my half-acquaintances are doing, which sometimes makes me sad. I missed a friend’s engagement announcement and had to say sorry using my mouth.

But this was unexpected. It brought boredom back. Fertile boredom. The kind where you realize you’ve been meaning to fix that wobbly chair for 2 years. So I did. And then sat there quietly, not taking a photo for anyone.

If you’re considering, you don’t need a better reason than wanting your own attention back. I waited 11 years for some excuse. Then realized it was enough to just ‘I wanted to.’

essay_opinion_02_sonnet.text:
I left a RTO fintech role in Charlotte in March 2024. Everyone thought it was about commuting.

It wasn't. 

It was about the "quick sync" at 11AM that lasted 90 minutes because our VP could not decide without explaining his internal reasoning to the 11 people in the room (4 of which didn't matter). 

We continue to fight the wrong war when it comes to remote/work. 

Execs will show badge swipe statistics and claim collaborative decay. 

Employees will cite their commute and insist on having 2 hrs per day back. 

Both sides are talking about location when the REAL problem is about time. 

As of 2023, Dropbox reported that employees averaged 21 hrs per week in meetings. 

Asana's "Anatomy of Work" has indicated for the past 3 years that over half of the meetings people are in are viewed as a waste of time.

Guess it didn't begin in 2020. 

Zoom didn't create the meeting that should've been an email. 

They just added a gallery view to it. 

I've been in offices that had meeting culture. 

Startup in Austin. Maybe 40 people. 

CEO made sure that if there wasn't an agenda for the meeting, his assistant would cancel. No appeal. 

They wanted to be there. 

No one was stealing back commute time from that office. 

Because there was value in the time spent inside. 

Whereas in the Charlotte role, calendar looked like a tetris board of forget-about-it-recurring-standups. 

Offices were ok. 

Good coffee. 

Nice espresso machine. 

Natural light on 9th floor. 

It wasn't about the building. 

It was about me spending 45 mins of my day watching someone read slides. 

RTO mandates assume you can create value by having people near each other. 

They continually fall short because they miss the thing. 

Salesforce. Amazon. Dell. 

Over the last couple years, they have really pushed on 5 days in office. 

Yet when they survey internally, the #1 gripe is meeting exhaustion, not missing their commute. 

You can force them into an office and they just have worse meetings in person vs remote. 

Same decay. 

Worse parking. 

If offices want to be relevant again, get rid of half of your recurring meetings. 

Not half your remote days.

i left a rto job (fintech in charlotte) in march 2024 and everyone thought it was the commute. it wasn't. it was the 11am "quick sync" that lasted 90 minutes because our vp couldn't make a decision without talking through his thought process aloud to 11 people, 4 of whom didn't even affect the outcome.

the rwo debate is always being fought in the wrong place. execs look at badging data and say we've lost collaborative powers. workers look at their commute and say 2 hours a day, no way. both sides are arguing over location. the disease is calendaring. dropbox did a study in 2023 and found that people spent on average 21 hours a week in meetings. for three years now asana has had the anatomy of work report showing that more than half of all meetings are seen as a waste of time. this is not a 2020-issue. zoom didn't create the meeting that could've been an email. it just created a gallery view.

i've worked in offices where we had great meeting etiquette (startup in austin, maybe 40 people, ceo had rule that if you didn't have a meeting agenda written down, his assistant cancelled it w/ no appeals). people wanted to be in the office. no one was trying to get their commute back there because the time inside was valuable. not my charlotte job where the calendar was a tetris board of forgotten recurring standups and the office itself was solid (good coffee, nice espresso machine, natural light on the 9th floor). it wasn't the building. it was 45 min of my day watching someone verbally process a slide.

rto mandate is betting on the proximity-value illusion and it's failing because the variable isn't looked at. salesforce, amazon, and dell have all been very forceful in bringing people back to 5 days a week in the past 2 years. yet survey results inside these orgs are still showing that meeting burnout is the #1 issue. not hating commutes. you can make someone come back to a building and they're just gonna have shitty meetings in person rather than over a screen. same shit, worse parking.

if orgs want to make offices important again, they need to cut half of their recurring meetings first, not half their remote days.

essay_opinion_04_luna.text:
Lesson 1 about digital nomads from Lisbon’s housing crisis: Living anywhere usually means living in a place you just drove up the price of.

October 2022. Suitcase and the usual pitch: working online, getting paid in dollars, wanted to live here, slow down. $1,500 monthly rent for an apartment in Arroios. More than many people here make. A steal because only a 3-month lease. Ex-tourist Airbnb (the landlord).

Cafes near Intendente and Graça. Other remote workers swap neighborhoods, Wi-Fi, visas. Dreamy talk of “community.” Almost never talk about who they displaced from the community. “My partner and I moved to Setúbal when they raised our rent €300,” a bartender said. Commute to central Lisbon almost 2 hours there and back. She wasn’t looking for a lifestyle. She was looking for a home.

The ugly reality is that digital nomadism is arbitrage through geography. We’re importing salaries from high-income economies into places with housing issues. As individuals, we’re polite, interested, recycling etc. As a whole, we can still make a place less liveable for the folks who made it.

Lisbon hasn’t taught me that foreigners are uniquely to blame for Lisbon’s housing crisis. Over many years there’s been speculation, AirBnB, weak tenant rights, stagnant wages. Outsiders like us aren’t the main factor. But we’re part of the demand. And we don’t always acknowledge it. We think of ourselves as flexible, but what we really are is spendy.

So now when I hear someone talking about how great it is to work from anywhere, I picture that bartender on her commute. Anywhere isn’t a blank canvas. It’s where there are schools, grandparents, rent control, people without return flights.

The most anti-digital nomad move I can think of is not just “can I live here?” but “what would happen if a bunch of folks like me decided we could?”

What I learned from Lisbon's housing crisis: the first lesson about digital nomads is that when you're "living anywhere", you're often living where other people can't afford to live anymore.

I moved to Lisbon in October 2022. Just a suitcase. The standard things: I worked online, I was paid in dollars, I wanted to take my time with this place. I found an apartment in Arroios for €1,150 a month (which was more than many people in Lisbon earned) - a steal because the rental term was only 3 months. Before this the owner was renting it to tourists on Airbnb.

I met more remote workers in cafes in Intendente, Graça. We'd compare areas, talk wifi, talk about visas. We'd gush about "community" but rarely about the people that community had displaced. I met a bartender who'd relocated to Setúbal with her partner when their rent went up by €300. It was almost 2 hours each way to central Lisbon. She wasn't looking for a lifestyle, she was looking for a place to live.

Digital nomadism is awkward because it's a way to arbitrage space. We bring salaries from richer places into already-tight housing markets. Individually we might be friendly, interested, responsible with our recycling. But en masse we can still destroy a neighborhood for the people who created it.

In Lisbon I didn't learn that foreigners are uniquely to blame for the housing crisis. It's more to do with years of speculation, short term rentals, inadequate tenant protection, stagnant wages than any particular wave of outsiders. But nomads are part of that demand - and we often mask that with the way we talk. We like to talk about being flexible. But we really mean that we have buying power.

Now when I hear people talk about the freedom of working anywhere, I think about that bartender's commute. Because "anywhere" isn't just a blank canvas. It's a place with schools, with grandparents, with rent control, with people that don't have a return flight.

The most un-digital nomad thing I can think of is asking not just "can I afford to live here?" but "what would happen if thousands of people like me decided they could live here too?".

essay_opinion_06_glm.text:
The first thing I do upon arriving Haneda Airport at 1am a Tuesday in March is go to 7-Eleven.

Onigiri. Salmon, ¥140, encased in plastic that keeps the nori fresh right up until you eat it, a design patented in the 70s and honed ever since.

I'm eating it on the streetcorner of Meguro, half-asleep, half-crazy.

Best fucking rice ball ever.

That's how it is with the convenience stores in Tokyo. Konbini. There's 56,000 in Japan. Over 7,000 in Tokyo. You can't be more than a few hundred meters from one.

We make fun of them. The soulless emblems of alienation. A hungry neon sign, burning all night.

But after living in Nakano for three years, I've come to respect the fucking genius of the konbini. It's one of the most advanced urban designs ever.

Look. The standard convenience store gets a new stock three times a day. Because the bento got made in the morning. Gets discounted in the evening.

They know shōgayaki pork is popular for lunch in Shinjuku. Not in Setagaya. They adjust by store.

Nothing goes stale. The food is fucking good. Karaage! Egg sandwiches! Oden bubbling on the counter in the winter!

I've eaten worse food in New York. For 3x the price.

But it's more than that. It's everything.

You can pay your utility bills. Print things out. Buy concert tickets. Mail things. Send luggage.

The ATM accepts foreign credit cards. Saved my ass multiple times.

During the pandemic when Tokyo's restaurants closed early, the konbini took all the city's mealtimes in stride.

When the government introduced the 2019 plastic bag fee, the konbini responded overnight.

But the thing that gets me...

It's the social aspect.

Old guy, 6:40am every morning. Coffee, Sankei Shimbun.

Just saying hello. The clerk knows him.

37M people. The konbini is Tokyo's corner store. Super-scaled. You'd think with terrifying precision.

Yet somehow, friendly.

We ask how to make cities more liveable. More walkable. More human.

Maybe it's this. On Koenji Dori, 3am. Superbright. Offering hot coffee. Fried chicken. Umbrellas. Nothing. Just 130 yen.

I walked into a 7-11 at 1am on a Tuesday in March after landing at Haneda. I bought an onigiri. Salmon. 140 yen. In plastic. (Patented in the 1970s. Developed for decades. The plastic is designed to keep the seaweed crunchy right up until you open the onigiri.) I ate it on the sidewalk in Meguro, jet-lagged and borderline insane, and I thought, holy fuck this is the best rice ball I've ever eaten.

This is what the Tokyo convenience stores (the konbini) are like. There are 56,000+ of them in Japan. 7,000+ in Tokyo. So you're never more than a few hundred meters from one. And so we laugh at them as an example of the modern alienating soul. The bright flashing beacon of convenience food that never sleeps. But I've lived in Nakano for 3 years, and the konbini is one of the most advanced, sophisticated urban systems on Earth.

For example, they restock at least 3 times a day. Because your bento is cooked that morning and on sale at night. They know a shogayaki pork lunch is popular in Shinjuku, but not in Setagaya, so they adjust accordingly, store by store. Everything is fresh. The food is very good! The karaage! The egg sandwiches! The oden bubbling away near the register in winter! I've paid 3x the price for worse food in NYC.

But it's not just the food. It's everything else. Pay your electricity bills. Print your documents. Buy your concert tickets. Send your luggage. (The ATMs accept foreign cards, which saved me a few times.) When Tokyo restaurants closed early during the pandemic, the konbini effortlessly swallowed Tokyo's eating times. When the government implemented its new plastic bag charge in 2019, the konbini adjusted instantly.

The thing I like most is the social aspect. When the old man walks in at 6:40am every morning to buy his coffee and Sankei Shimbun newspaper, he's not just getting breakfast. He's saying hello. The clerk knows him. Among the 37 million people, the konbini is Tokyo's equivalent of the corner shop. Though with an almost freakishly precise scale. And yet it feels warm.

How can we make cities in the West more liveable? More walkable? More human? Maybe we should think about standing on the corner of Koenji Dori at 3am in the fully lit glow, offering hot coffee and fried chicken and umbrellas, expecting nothing more than 130 yen from you.

essay_opinion_08_sonnet.text:
My sis-in-law ran a dried flower shop Petal & Pine out of her 400 sq ft storefront in Asheville. The landlord jacked the rent 100% in March 2025. She packed everything into a storage unit on Sweeten Creek Road and locked up the storefront. I thought that was it. But then her daughter Reyna (22) hijacked the dormant IG, wiped it and set up a TikTok with 0 followers. 
 Fast forward 11 months, Petal & Pine is now national, 340k in gross sales last year. Most of it via one account belonging to a 2024 studio art grad who, by all boomers' standards, has no business acumen. 
 I saw it happen, and it didn't look lazy. It looked like a self-imposed apprenticeship. 
 She shared the flops ($600 wholesale flower order that showed up moldy, shipping mistake that ended up in Ontario instead of Ohio) because she'd discovered (not at business school) that posting "process" beats perfectly shot products four-to-one. That through watching 200 other small shop owners crash and burn in public and comparing notes in a Discord with 40 or so strangers that now serve as her supply chain, focus group, therapist. She measures watch-time retention like mom used to measure foot traffic. Within a day she knows which color palette will sell. Because she tested the same arrangement to three different audiences and reviewed completion rates as if it was a P&L. 
 It isn't the entitled lazy stereotype I grew up reading about in a decade's worth of trend stories. It's more like my dad's business in the '80s hardware store. Read the room. Shift stock. Cultivate relationships with the 15 that would vouch for you. Except the room is 900k followers. And you cultivate relationships by commenting in comment threads at 11 PM. 
 This isn't happening because the traditional "clerking register and waiting for people to come" job isn't available in much of retail anymore. I let AI write my wedding toast (because three days before the wedding I only had 47 words and they didn't even make sense together)

June 14, Conservatory Garden, Central Park. My sister, Lena, is getting married to Marcus (after 8 years together), and somehow I'm supposed to speak eloquently in front of 86 people (including our terrifyingly-fluent grandmother). I know that Lena drove 4 hours to return Marcus's lost passport once. I know Marcus learned to bake Lena's mom's cardamom bread. I know they adopted a one-eyed cat (name: Pickle). But my sentences all sound like they're on a greeting card.

So I start an AI chatbot and I write: Write a warm, funny wedding toast for my sister Lena and her husband Marcus. Include cardamom bread, Pickle, and how they make each other braver.

The AI spat out a beautiful speech in seconds. A good one! A infuriatingly good one. One that had a beat, and a joke (about Pickle being "the real head of the household") and a line about how love doesn't simplify life, but makes difficult things worth doing. I steal most of it and put it in my notes.

At the reception, there are lots of chuckles at the right moments. Lena's crying before I am. Marcus gives me a hug afterwards and says, "that was perfect."

But on the train ride home, I sort of feel like I've stolen an emotion.

This was my toast, factually. I had the memories. I gave all the necessary ingredients. But it was the sentences - the words that were heard - were not from something that's ever seen Lena salsa in our parents' kitchen barefoot. Or seen Marcus sit by her at an emergency room at 2:17 am. This thing knows what a wedding toast is supposed to sound like. It doesn't know them.

Maybe that's not such a big deal. Humans have always taken other forms. Poems. Vows. Jokes. Prayers. We use templates because the feelings are often too big to mold from scratch. The machine provided the ladder. I had to climb it.

I'm glad for the toast. And I'm going to hang on to the 47 words too. Clunky but mine.

We first tried it for 4 days back in October - mostly due to our operations director (Priya) spamming us with articles about it. 22 of us at a logistics software company in Leeds - and we were having staff turnover (3 resignations over the summer). So one foggy Tuesday, the directors dropped this on us: we're going to close every Friday for the next 6 months and see what happens.

I imagined chaos. But it turned out to be more subtle and profound. The Death Of The Pretend Meeting.

This is what they don't tell you about the 4 day week. It wasn't the 5th day that was hard. It was how much of our 4 days we were pretending. Monday morning's status call - 90 minutes? New cut-off is 25 mins. Now everyone's got places to be (theirs, presumably). All those "quick syncs" that actually turned into people refusing to make decisions in writing? No more. By November, team chat developed an unwritten rule - if it can be said in a message, then it is a message.

We also saw metrics improve. 14% faster response time to customer tickets (not because we worked faster, but because Tom finally had time to fix the ticket routing process he'd been "planning to do" for two years). We got the space to work on things like that on Fridays off - except we didn't do that. We did that because we had the space to work on things guilt-free due to the existence of Friday.

But in reality, it was a cultural shift - subtle furniture rearrangement. People were saying they didn't know what to do. Maybe because with a 4 day week, you are implicitly promised - we respect your time, we're not going to waste it. Once you are promised that, then it's dumber to waste your own time too. Marcus (our junior dev) asked for help on a problem in week 2. He told me he'd normally wait a month to ask.

Not everything went smooth. Two clients initially hated it that we weren't around on Fridays, until we tweaked their support rotation. Dillon kept working from home on Fridays anyway - out of habit. It took a direct conversation to point out that the goal wasn't to cram 5 days in 4.

In April, the end of the trial, it was 21-1 to make it permanent. Dillon voted yes.

I don't think of it as a scheduling thing any more. It was a truth thing. You shrink the week - you shrink the excuses. Turned out a lot of our "collaborative" work was just mutual avoidance, but with a calendar invite.

Every single person is still talking about the energy transition like it's a product launch in the Bay Area — a Tesla being pulled into a driveway, a heat pump startup doing Demo Day. The actual work of retrofitting the US to generate and transport electrons is getting done in Houston, on Allen Parkway and along the Katy Freeway, within the very same companies that used to just ... pump oil. 
 NRG Energy is headquartered downtown. And so is Quanta Services, which last year installed more grid infrastructure than you probably realize exists. Exxon's low-carbon solutions business announced in 2021 is now based in the same campus as its upstream business. That's where they're going for carbon capture contracts on the Houston Ship Channel — the biggest single cluster of CO2 point sources in the United States. And that's a perfect place to build your CCS infrastructure because... well, it's the best place on Earth to build CCS infrastructure. The Greater Houston Partnership has 400+ companies in the region now working on hydrogen, wind, solar and carbon management. A lot of these are spinouts and pivots from companies who spent fifty years doing seismic surveys and pipe engineering. 
 The thing Silicon Valley doesn't communicate that well: it's not a software thing. On Tuesday night at 8:47pm, I placed an order for milk, bananas, and a sack of rice via QuickCart, the 15-minute grocery delivery app. At 8:59, a guy with a blue helmet delivered it to my front door on Valencia Street. It was magical. That is, until I saw him sprinting back to his e-bike, already tapping the next notification.

In this neighborhood, the 15-minute window is altering the streets. Ever since QuickCart and DashBasket built dark grocery warehouses nearby (2024), delivery guys are hanging around all the corner markets, their bikes clogging the curb cuts and bus stops. They ride in the rain, the heat, and the late-night dead. They earn by the delivery, and incur a fine, if several riders I've asked are to be believed, if they deliver late. Convenience is often someone else's burden.

There's a human price to pay for making eggs a matter of urgency. Peddling through traffic on Valencia and 24th, they're racing the timer on the app. I've seen them take the sidewalk when a van was double parked. Sit outside on a December night. Apartment lobbies are locked. I heard one guy made $118 in 10 hours last Saturday, minus expenses. Not even the cost of a single battery for a delivery scooter, much less San Francisco rent.

And a neighborhood price. The local markets that used to know their customers now compete with ones that have millions in venture capital investment and cater to spur of the moment purchases. No café. No bulletin board. No old-timer asking how your family's doing. Just sleek, efficient boxes built to monetize your hunger, your absent-mindedness, your boredom.

I still use it. Sometimes my disabled neighbor needs groceries. I remember at 9pm I'm out of medicine and can't get home from work. But I'm trying to be honest about what "instant" is. It doesn't make food happen quicker. It just puts the hassle on someone else, on a bike, in traffic, for a salary that scarcely lets you stay in the city. Groceries in 15 minutes? Sure. But, as always, the bill's coming in the mail.

When President Truman signed the European Recovery Program (aka Marshall Plan) into law on April 3, 1948, the economic prospects for West Germany seemed grim. West German industrial towns were rubble. The currency was practically worthless. And the economy remained shackled to occupation-era Allied policy limiting steel output and breaking up industrial facilities. But in the succeeding four years, West Germany (soon to become the Federal Republic) received about $1.4 billion in Marshall Plan aid that catalyzed one of the most stunning economic comebacks of the 20th century.

The Marshall Plan aid provided by the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) had less to do with the size of the aid than with its timing and function. The Marshall Plan provided goods (cotton, wheat, coal, machinery, etc.) to West Germany which were purchased with virtually worthless Reichsmarks that were in turn deposited in a special counterpart fund. That fund, a few billion Deutschmarks, was in turn invested in infrastructure and industry to support such things as the modernization of the electrical grid and expansion of the steel industry in the Ruhr Valley. And perhaps equally important was the Marshall Plan aid which in 1949 and 1950 helped support Germany's persistent trade deficit, giving breathing room to the young West German government during the adjustment period of its currency reform in June 1948 (which introduced the Deutschmark).

The Marshall Plan also led to important institutional changes. In order to receive US aid, West Germany had to join the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC), bringing West Germany into a European cooperation that led to the 1951 European Coal and Steel Community decades later. Also, US pressure relaxed some occupation restrictions, incrementally boosting the steel production quota from about 5.8 million tons to over 11 million tons by the early 1950s, while dismantling industrial plants was more or less stopped. Meanwhile, the new Economic Director (1948) Ludwig Erhard combined these new opportunities with his policy of the "social market economy," which integrated free-market competition with social safety-nets.

Between 1948 and 1952, West German industrial production approximately doubled. By the mid-1950s West Germany was producing more than it did before the war. The Chancellor Konrad Adenauer's government called this phenomenon the "economic miracle" (Wirtschaftswunder). Of course, historians are careful to note that the Marshall Plan was only one of several reasons for West Germany's recovery (the others being the currency reform, the Korean War-driven demand, and the availability of skilled labor). But it's fair to say that the US aid didn't only repair West Germany's economy, it re-directed the economy. Re-directed towards Europe, trade and stable, democratic capitalism that was to be the Federal Republic's hallmark for decades to come.

On April 3, 1948, President Truman signed the law to create the European Recovery Program, otherwise known as the Marshall Plan. The economic prospects for West Germany at the time seemed desperate. The country’s industrial cities were rubble, the currency nearly worthless, and the economy bound by Allied occupation measures that restricted steel output and dismantled industries. But for the next four years, the Federal Republic of Germany (as the country would become) received about $1.4 billion in Marshall Plan aid to help set the stage for what would be one of the most stunning economic recoveries of the 20th century.

But the Marshall Plan aid delivered by the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) did not merely provide funds. As much or more important was its timing and purpose. In effect, West Germany received goods—cotton, wheat, coal, and machinery, etc.—purchased in nearly worthless Reichsmarks that then went to a special counterpart fund. Later, this fund (several billion Deutschmarks) was used to reinvest in German infrastructure and industry, helping fund modernization of the electrical grid and the steel industry’s expansion in the Ruhr Valley, for example. Just as significantly, the Marshall Plan money addressed Germany’s persistent trade deficit problem in 1949 and 1950 while allowing time for West Germany’s currency reform of June 1948 to take hold (introducing the Deutschmark).

Marshall Plan aid also helped compel important institutional changes. In exchange for accepting U.S. aid, West Germany had to join the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC), bringing West Germany into a structure of European cooperation that would lead decades later to the 1951 European Coal and Steel Community. And U.S. pressure was a factor in relaxing occupation controls. Restrictions on steel output were gradually increased from roughly 5.8 million tons to over 11 million tons by the early 1950s, for example. And the dismantling of industries largely ended. With this newfound latitude, Economic Director (appointed in 1948) Ludwig Erhard combined the new direction with his program for the “social market economy” that mixed free market competition with a social safety net.

The results were dramatic. Between 1948 and 1952, West German industrial production approximately doubled. By the mid-1950s, West Germany’s output exceeded prewar levels. This postwar boom was known as the Wirtschaftswunder or “economic miracle” and was trumpeted by Chancellor Konrad Adenauer’s government. As historians point out, the Marshall Plan was only one of several contributing factors—along with currency reform, demand for Korean War products, and the availability of a skilled workforce. But it is certainly true that U.S. aid did more than simply restore West Germany’s economy. It fundamentally reconfigured it. It reconfigured West Germany for Europe. For trade. For the enduring form of stable democratic capitalism that would characterize the Federal Republic for decades.

essay_student_04_luna.text: In Pride and Prejudice (1813), Jane Austen takes issue with the unfair inheritance practices that make women vulnerable. The Bennet family owns Longbourn in Hertfordshire, which is "entailed" to the male line, meaning that at the death of Mr. Bennet his five daughters (Jane, Elizabeth, Mary, Kitty and Lydia) are unable to inherit it. Instead, their distant cousin, Mr. William Collins, will inherit the property. This is why Mrs. Bennet is always worried that her daughters need to marry rich, because they cannot secure their financial future by inheriting family property. Austen demonstrates how the system of inheritance can make marriage an economic imperative, rather than just a personal choice. When Mr. Collins comes to call, this issue becomes even more apparent. Mr. Collins is an unintelligent and tactless man, but he has a future legal right to Longbourn. When Elizabeth refuses to marry him, her mother worries that Elizabeth has made a stupid mistake that will jeopardise the family's future. Charlotte Lucas, aged twenty-seven with few financial prospects, agrees to marry Mr. Collins, because it will give her a secure home and social stability. Austen doesn't portray Charlotte as romantic, but she does portray her as a reasonable woman in an unfair economic situation. The ramifications of the inequality in inheritance are made even starker when Lydia elopes with Mr. Wickham. If Lydia does not marry well, then her actions could ruin the reputation and future prospects of her sisters. The women of the Bennet family are not the victims of their circumstances because they are stupid or immoral: instead they are victims of a system that takes away their property rights and leaves their security at the mercy of men. Austen is not explicitly political in her critique, but she uses irony, awkward conversations, and contrasts between sensible Elizabeth and silly Mr. Collins to show that the so-called respectable society promotes male inheritance and forces women to play the game of survival. Despite the fact that Elizabeth ends up marrying Mr. Darcy and is financially secure, the fact that she needed to be financially secure doesn't change the unfairness of the situation.

Jane Austen was not a politically engaged writer, but in Pride and Prejudice (1813), she attacks the unfair inheritance laws that leave women poor and powerless. The Bennets live in Longbourn, in the county of Hertfordshire. Their family property is "entailed", that is to say, it is inherited by the male line. When Mr. Bennet dies, it will not be inherited by his five daughters: Jane, Elizabeth, Mary, Kitty and Lydia. Instead it will go to Mr. William Collins, a distant relative. This is why Mrs. Bennet is always worrying that her daughters should find rich husbands. They won't have any property to fall back on for security, since they won't inherit. Jane Austen illustrates the economic importance of marriage, which should not only be a matter of choice but of economic necessity. The arrival of Mr. Collins highlights the issues involved. Mr. Collins is a silly and insensitive man, but in the future he will be the legal owner of Longbourn. When he proposes to Elizabeth and she refuses, Mrs. Bennet thinks she has stupidly jeopardised the family's security. Charlotte Lucas, an unattractive woman of twenty-seven with few options, marries Mr. Collins. She needs somewhere to live and some social protection. Although Jane Austen does not portray her as romantic, she shows that Charlotte has to do what she does because of the unfairness of the economic system. When Lydia elopes with Mr. Wickham, the problems of an unequal inheritance become even more critical. If Lydia is not married respectably, her bad behaviour might ruin all the sisters' reputations and prospects. The Bennets women are not foolish or stupid, they are the victims of the unfair laws that don't give them property rights and leave their fate in the hands of men. Austen doesn't attack inequality directly. She is a subtle writer. She uses irony, awkward dialogue and the contrast between the intelligent Elizabeth and the stupid Mr. Collins to show how a supposedly civilised society endorses male inheritance and forces women to wriggle about to stay alive. On December 1, 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks, an African American woman, quietly resisted racial segregation by refusing to give up her bus seat to a white man. This moment of resistance would ignite a pivotal shift in the American civil rights movement. Unlike the common narrative of Parks simply being a tired seamstress, she was a skilled organizer, acting as secretary of the Montgomery branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), and her defiance was intentional, fully aware of the possible outcome. She was arrested and fined according to Montgomery’s segregation codes, but her arrest would trigger events beyond anyone's imagination.

Almost immediately, activists like Jo Ann Robinson of the Women's Political Council began to print and circulate around 35,000 flyers advocating for a one-day boycott of city buses on December 5, 1955. The boycott was so effective that a group of community leaders established the Montgomery Improvement Association to carry the movement forward, electing a young 26-year-old pastor, Martin Luther King Jr., as their president. What started as a protest against segregated buses evolved into a 381-day effort, where approximately 40,000 Black citizens in Montgomery walked, carpooled, and faced harassment and violence, refusing to ride on segregated buses. Despite the bombing of King's house and many boycotters losing their jobs or being arrested, the community persevered.

The boycott concluded on December 20, 1956, when the Supreme Court affirmed a lower court decision in Browder v. Gayle that bus segregation was unconstitutional. This milestone proved that collective mass nonviolent resistance could break down the structures of discrimination, and it elevated King to national recognition, eventually leading to the founding of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference in 1957.

The Montgomery Bus Boycott is a cornerstone in civil rights history, not just for its successful legal outcome but for its foundational role in creating a new kind of activism that would shape the following decade. It demonstrated that individuals—housekeepers, teachers, students—had the power to resist an unfair system through organized and strategic action. Rosa Parks' bravery set off the match, but the real flame was the relentless determination of the Black community in Montgomery. As Parks herself would later say, "the only tired I was, was tired of giving in." Her arrest, and the movement that followed, showed that sometimes, it only takes a refusal to move in order to resist injustice.

In June of 2013, a then 29 year-old Booz Allen Hamilton contractor at the National Security Agency’s Hawaii headquarters, Edward Snowden, turned over to journalists Glenn Greenwald and Laura Poitras thousands of classified files describing operations such as PRISM and bulk surveillance of U.S. phone data under Section 215 of the Patriot Act. Published on June 6, 2013, in The Guardian, these revelations sparked an international discussion of privacy, surveillance, and the bounds of state secrets. It also raised a more complex question: when, if at all, should one choose to break one’s sworn oath and the law to report wrongdoing?

In favor of Snowden’s actions, consider the principle of consequences and moral obligation. Snowden’s leaks exposed NSA’s collection of metadata on millions of Americans without individualized suspicion, a program deemed “almost Orwellian” by a federal judge, Richard Leon, later that year. Such whistleblowing can be crucial when internal methods fail. As Snowden himself has noted, he voiced his concerns to others, believing any official report would be ignored or used against him. The utilitarian approach may support Snowden’s actions, as the consequences of disclosure were judged less harmful than the broader good of transparency, discourse, and, ultimately, change — like the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015 that ended bulk phone record collection.

On the other hand, Snowden clearly broke the Espionage Act of 1917, swore an oath to preserve classified information, and fled first to Hong Kong and, since 2013, to Moscow, prompting questions of whether he acted for moral purity or self-preservation. Deontological thinkers will point to the importance of laws and oaths: if an intelligence agent can unilaterally determine what secrets society should know, then precedents are set that can lead to life-threatening outcomes or stifle necessary security measures. Critics of Snowden’s actions, such as former NSA Director Michael Hayden, contended that Snowden had other legal means to act (e.g., the Intelligence Community Whistleblower Protection Act), even if those avenues were imperfect.

The ethical problem is complex, as it involves the collision of two goods: the rule of law and trust in institutions versus the public’s need to know when a government exceeds its own covert boundaries. The Snowden example hints that whistleblowing can be valid only in limited circumstances: if the wrongdoing is widespread, the damage great, and the internal process exhausted. On this account, Snowden’s actions appear less like treason or heroism, and more like a strategic risk that the truth would be worth his known personal consequences.

In June 2013, a 29-year-old Booz Allen Hamilton contractor at the National Security Agency's Hawaii facility, Edward Snowden, leaked thousands of sensitive documents to journalists Glenn Greenwald and Laura Poitras, exposing programs such as PRISM and mass surveillance of U.S. phone data under Section 215 of the Patriot Act. First reported by The Guardian on June 6, 2013, the leaks sparked global discussions on surveillance, privacy, and the boundaries of state secrecy. But they also raised a crucial moral question: under what circumstances is it acceptable to breach a sacred oath and the law to reveal misconduct?

Snowden's defense lies in the principles of consequence and conscience. He exposed NSA's mass collection of metadata on millions of Americans without specific suspicion, a practice labeled "almost Orwellian" by federal judge Richard Leon later in 2013. Whistleblowing is critical because formal systems may not work; Snowden reportedly voiced his concerns internally, but felt any formal complaints would be dismissed or used against him. On a utilitarian approach, Snowden's actions could be justified as the lesser of two evils: the potential damage from exposure was outweighed by the greater good of accountability, public discourse, and reform (such as the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015, which dismantled the bulk phone record collection).

However, Snowden faces significant objections. He broke the Espionage Act of 1917, swore an oath to safeguard classified information, and fled to Hong Kong and then to Moscow, where he has resided since 2013. This raises doubts about his motivations: was he acting from principle, or merely safeguarding his own interests? Deontologists argue that laws and oaths hold intrinsic moral value; when an intelligence officer unilaterally determines what information is fit for public disclosure, it sets a dangerous precedent that could cost lives or disrupt necessary operations. Some detractors, like former NSA Director Michael Hayden, pointed out Snowden could have taken legal steps (e.g., under the Intelligence Community Whistleblower Protection Act) though imperfect.

The moral dilemma of Snowden is difficult to settle because it involves conflicting goods: the sanctity of law and institutional confidence, or the public's need to be informed when a government abuses its own secrecy. The Snowden affair hints that whistleblowing may be acceptable only if: (1) the wrongdoing is systemic, (2) the harm is serious, and (3) internal recourse has been fully exhausted. By these criteria, Snowden's actions may not have been treason or heroism, but rather a risky play, wagering that the truth was worth the inevitable fallout he anticipated.

Scott Fitzgerald's 1925 novel, The Great Gatsby, is representative of Jay Gatsby's dreams, particularly his dreams of being with Daisy again and reliving their past. Gatsby lives in West Egg on the bay opposite East Egg where Daisy lives, and Gatsby often extends his arm toward the faint green light that gleams on Daisy's dock. The green light is within Gatsby's visual reach, but the expanse of water between him and Daisy stands as a barrier of emotion, class and time. Gatsby sees that he can transcend those barriers with money, and so he erects a mansion, throws wild parties and becomes wealthy to catch Daisy's eye. The green light signifies the American Dream too because Gatsby thinks that happiness is just around the bend. Like so many who strive for something greater, Gatsby feels that if he could just reach another goal, his life would be complete. Green represents hope, renewal and passion but it also represents money, making Daisy's dream for Gatsby a dream of wealth too. Gatsby wants to buy love, status with money. Eventually Nick Carraway, the narrator, comes to see that Gatsby's dream is a romanticized memory, not reality. Gatsby doesn't want Daisy as she is now in 1922, he wants to reclaim the romance he and Daisy had before he went off to fight in World War I and before Daisy married Tom. Gatsby's famous statement about bringing the past back demonstrates the extent of his confusion of hope and possibility. By the end of the novel, Gatsby is dead, Daisy has left him and the green light still blazes on the bay. The significance of the green light has broadened from Gatsby's dream to a symbol of the country's never-ending quest for a fantasy future. Fitzgerald's concluding scene of men and women laboring forward while being forced backward emphasizes the inspiring and tragic nature of the green light, how it enables individuals to dream but also to refuse the actual.

At the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock in the 1925 novel The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald is a green light that signifies Jay Gatsby's aspirations, particularly the aspiration of getting back together with Daisy Buchanan and reliving their old romance. West Egg, the house where Gatsby lives, sits on the other side of the bay from East Egg, the home of Daisy Buchanan. Gatsby can often be seen stretching out to touch the distant green light that glows at the tip of Daisy's dock. Though the light is close enough to see, the gulf of water between Daisy and Gatsby separates them emotionally, socially, and historically. Gatsby thinks money can bridge that gap. So he builds a huge house, throws enormous parties, and makes a lot of money in the hopes that Daisy will take notice. But in addition to signifying the American Dream, which suggests that the good life is just out of reach, the green light symbolizes Gatsby's dreams. As with many ambitious people, he thinks that if he can just attain another goal, then his life will finally be perfect. The green of the light signifies hope, rejuvenation, and aspiration--but also money. The money theme associates Gatsby's fantasy of Daisy with the idea that he can buy her love and social status. Eventually, however, Nick Carraway discovers that Gatsby's dream is a kind of fantasy based on memory. Gatsby doesn't want just 1922 Daisy. What he really wants is to re-create the romance that he and Daisy had before he went off to fight in World War I and before she married Tom. His famous claim that the past can be repeated makes clear that he mistakes hope for possibility to an extreme degree. In the end of the novel, Gatsby is dead, Daisy has left him, and the green light still burns across the bay. The significance of the light has now broadened to include not just Gatsby's dream, but a nation's ongoing quest for a dream that has yet to be realized. Fitzgerald's last image of people trudging along while they're being dragged back suggests that the green light is both alluring and tragic--it gives people something to aim for but may also keep them from coming to terms with what is.

The catastrophy of Napoleon's Russian invasion of 1812 could have been prevented. It was, rather, a series of decisions, primarily Napoleon's. The Russian campaign was sparked by a political disagreement which was not a sufficient cause for this kind of war: The Russian Tsar Alexander I threw off the Continental System, Napoleon's blockade of Britain, because it was suffocating trade in Russian goods like lumber and tallow. Napoleon didn't want to try negotiation, nor compromise, so he mustered up the Grande Armée, some 600,000 men, the greatest army in European history, and on June 24, 1812, he forded the Neman.

To begin with, the catastrophy was preventable because it was very ill-timed. Napoleon invaded in late June, hoping he could win a decisive battle and force Alexander to beg for peace within a few weeks. But the Russians under Barclay de Tolly, then Mikhail Kutuzov, would not be caught. Instead they retreated eastward, burning supplies as they retreated. It turned into a victory-less pursuit. Napoleon arrived in Moscow in September, after the costly (70,000 casualties total) victory at Borodino on Sept 7. Only to find Moscow in flames and Alexander unwilling to negotiate. Such an intelligent emperor as Napoleon should have had backup plans for this type of thing, but he stayed in Moscow more than a month waiting for a letter that didn't come, until the winter set in and he had to march out.

Second, the logistics were well known to be insufficient. Napoleon expected to supply his army partly from magazines and partly from foraging. But the Russian scorched earth policy and the long distances made this impossible. Tens of thousands of horses died. Typhus and dysentery ravaged the army before any major battle. Of the 600,000 men who went into Russia, an estimated 100,000 came out. A smaller army with supply lines or even a smaller scale campaign (say, limited to Lithuania/Belorussia) would probably have brought about a negotiated peace, without the catastrophy.

Pro-Napoleon people can point out that, as hegemon of Europe, Napoleon needed to enforce the Continental System, and a Russian refusal would provoke defections in Austria and Prussia if not taken seriously. That's somewhat true, but it's the reason for the invasion, not how it was conducted. Alternatives would have been diplomatic pressure, a demonstration force in Poland, or even a punitive expedition (smaller).

The invasion was a preventable catastrophy, due to overconfidence, bad intel and Napoleon's failure to believe his adversary might not want to play along. Russia didn't beat him on the battlefield; his own ideas beat him.

Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 was not a foregone conclusion, but a series of consequences of decisions made (especially by Napoleon). The trigger for the invasion was a political dispute that didn't warrant war on the grand scale: Russia's Tsar Alexander I broke out of Napoleon's Continental System (blockade of Britain) because it was choking off Russian trade of goods like wood and tallow. Instead of bargaining or compromising, Napoleon mustered the Grande Armée (some 600,000 troops, the largest army Europe had ever seen) and crossed the Neman River on June 24, 1812. 
 The disaster was preventable on several levels: 
 1) The timing was reckless. Napoleon invaded in late June, banking on the possibility of a quick crushing victory that would make Alexander ask for peace in a few weeks. With Russians (first Barclay de Tolly and then Mikhail Kutuzov) not taking the bait, retreating east and burning supplies, Napoleon had a game of tag. He finally got to Moscow in September (with the hard-won battle of Borodino on Sept. 7, 70,000 casualties in all), but found the city burning and Alexander unwilling to negotiate. A smart guy like Napoleon should have had plans B,C,D. for this sort of situation; instead he sat on his thumbs in Moscow for more than a month awaiting a letter that didn't come, until winter set in and he had to get out. 
 2) Napoleon knowingly used inadequate logistics. Napoleon's plan was to feed his army partially from magazines and partially by foraging, but that wasn't feasible given the scorched earth tactics of the Russians and the huge distances. Tens of thousands of horses perished, typhus and dysentery swept through the ranks even before the first big battle. Probably less than 100,000 out of 600,000 made it back, according to historians. A smaller expeditionary force with solid supply lines, or a raid limited to Lithuania/Belorussia, might have brought a deal without disaster. 
 Those who defend Napoleon say he had to make the Continental System work because he was a hegemon of Europe, and if Russia got away with it, Austria and Prussia might quit too. There's some truth to that, but it's not an argument for how the invasion was carried out. Diplomatic tactics, display of strength in Poland, even a punitive raid of lesser scope could have been options. 
 So the invasion was a preventable disaster: overconfidence, inadequate intelligence, inability to conceive of the other guy just not going along with your game. Russia didn't beat him in battle so much as his expectations did.
