On the evening of 9 November 1989, the East German spokesman Günter Schabowski accidentally declared that new rules would be introduced "immediately" when in fact they had planned a gradual controlled opening. Thousands of people gathered at checkpoints like Bornholmer Strasse and confused border guards without orders opened the gates. By the next morning thousands of East and West Berliners were dancing on top of the Wall by the Brandenburg Gate and picking at it with hammers.

The fall of the Berlin Wall was no random fluke but the logical conclusion of decades of building pressure. The policies of glasnost and perestroika introduced by Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev reduced the power that Moscow could exert in Eastern Europe. In 1989 he also made it clear that unlike 1956 in Hungary or 1968 in Czechoslovakia the Soviet Union would not send in troops to shore up satellite governments. Hungary itself had already removed its border fence with Austria in May, creating an escape route for East Germans to head West. In East Germany itself massive demonstrations were taking place, with more than 70,000 participating in the Monday marches in Leipzig by 9 October and by early November more than half a million gathering in East Berlin. The hardline leader Erich Honecker, in power in East Germany since 1971, was forced to resign in mid-October, and his successor Egon Krenz could not stop the situation from falling apart.

The implications of the events were swift and profound. Less than a year later, on 3 October 1990, East and West Germany formally merged under the leadership of Chancellor Helmut Kohl. The events also hastened the disintegration of communist rule in the Eastern Bloc: Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution was successful in a matter of weeks. By December 1989 Nicolae Ceaușescu's regime in Romania had collapsed in a bloody revolution. Reunification was also a significant economic burden: trillions of deutsche marks needed to be transferred to bring the former East Germany up to standard. The debate on this issue still rages among economists to this day. From a political perspective the fall of the Wall is often considered the symbolic end of the Cold War, which was officially sealed when the Soviet Union itself broke up in December 1991. A bureaucratic faux pas in a press conference had turned into a major turning point in the history of the 20th century.

East German spokesman Günter Schabowski mistakenly announced on November 9, 1989 that the new rules allowing travel would go into effect "immediately" -- though what was actually planned was a later, orderly opening. People rushed to border crossings such as Bornholmer Strasse; because the border guards were overwhelmed and didn't know what to do, they opened the gates. By that evening, thousands of East and West Berliners were dancing on top of the Wall, near the Brandenburg Gate, and smashing off chunks with sledge hammers.

The Berlin Wall did not fall out of the blue. It had been crumbling for several years, in part because Mikhail Gorbachev's policy of glasnost and perestroika was weakening Moscow's control over Eastern Europe. In 1989, Gorbachev had declared that the Soviet Union wouldn't intervene militarily to support its satellite states, as it had in 1956 in Hungary and 1968 in Czechoslovakia. Back in May, Hungary had torn down its border fence with Austria, opening a way for East Germans to escape to the West. In East Germany, huge demonstrations had been taking place: more than 70,000 were attending the Leipzig Monday demonstrations by October 9. By early November, more than a half million people were demonstrating in East Berlin. Hard-line East German leader Erich Honecker, in power since 1971, was ousted in mid-October. His replacement, Egon Krenz, could do nothing to stem the tide.

The fall of the Berlin Wall had profound and immediate effects. On October 3, 1990 -- less than a year later -- the two Germanys formally reunified, with Chancellor Helmut Kohl in power. The fall of the Wall also hastened the downfall of communist regimes in the Eastern Bloc. Within weeks, Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution had succeeded; by December 1989, Nicolae Ceaușescu's regime in Romania had come crashing down, violently. The economic effects of German reunification would be expensive; the massive (trillions of deutsche marks) transfers needed to bring the former East Germany up to date are a topic of debate among economists today. On the political level, the fall of the Berlin Wall is often seen as a symbolic end to the Cold War, which was made official when the Soviet Union itself broke apart in December 1991. A single press conference official's slip of the tongue had produced one of the 20th century's great historical turning points.

Driving for Uber in 2020 felt like freedom. Until the COVID-19 pandemic taught us the downside of that freedom—how it could also be a way to get exploited. Drive for Uber, and you could work when you want, refuse rides, earn money with an app instead of a boss. That seemed attractive to people who lost their jobs in restaurants or stores or offices. But then you had to buy your own gasoline. Pay for your own car maintenance. Pay for your own insurance. Pay for the hours you spend waiting for customers. Plus, Uber drivers were classified as contractors. So most likely they didn't get paid time off for illness. Or get unemployment. Or have employer-paid health insurance.

So when lockdowns in March and April 2020 cut down on travel a lot, risks for Uber drivers increased a lot. Uber said its rides business had fallen by about 80 percent year over year in April. Yet drivers had to worry about potentially spreading the coronavirus from one rider to the next. Uber said it was giving drivers and delivery workers around the world $24 million in assistance, but the help was hard to get for many workers and not nearly enough. And Uber required masks and new safety protocols. That could leave drivers feeling it was up to them to protect themselves.

This was particularly clear in California, where Assembly Bill 5, enacted in 2019, put up new roadblocks for companies using contractors. For Uber and Lyft, drivers wanted to be free. And Uber and Lyft began a massive push to make Proposition 22 pass. On November 3, 2020, Californians voted in favor. That meant app-based drivers would remain contractors. And Proposition 22 promised some benefits, like a healthcare subsidy, paid for hours drivers were engaged in trips. Proposition 22 supporters, including Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, claimed it would give drivers freedom. But critics said it let profitable tech companies off the hook for what comes with being an employer.

So in 2020 Uber drivers felt freedom. And they also felt exploitation. Uber gave them the freedom to choose when to drive. But they didn't get to choose the price. Or the costs. Or the health risks. Or the benefits. You can only have freedom if drivers can continue to pick their own hours and also have greater protection against sickness, car accidents, and economic insecurity. The lesson of 2020 is that freedom doesn't matter if workers have to bear almost all of the risk while companies hold almost all of the power.

In 2020, driving for Uber seemed a choice between freedom and exploitation, but the COVID-19 pandemic showed that freedom could be a form of exploitation. Driving for Uber seemed to offer flexibility—the driver chose his or her hours, could turn down jobs, could use the app to make money without a traditional boss. Many Uber drivers were laid off from the restaurant, retail, or office work they did before; for them, Uber seemed a source of flexibility. But the drivers had to spend their own money on gas, car maintenance, insurance, and downtime waiting for fares. They were also independent contractors, and therefore generally had no paid sick days, unemployment benefits, or an employer-provided health insurance.

The downside seemed like a trap in March and April of 2020, when lockdowns caused travel to plummet. Uber said its rides were down about 80 percent year over year in April. Meanwhile, drivers remained at risk of transporting the coronavirus from passenger to passenger. Uber announced $24 million in assistance for drivers and delivery workers around the world, but the help was thin and hard for many drivers to get. Uber required masks and took some other safety steps, but it also tried to pass some of the burden onto drivers for their own safety.

In California, where a 2019 law (Assembly Bill 5) had made it more difficult for firms to classify workers as independent contractors, the struggle played out in high relief. Uber and Lyft said drivers wanted the freedom. They ran an intense campaign in favor of Proposition 22. On November 3, 2020, California voters passed Prop. 22, allowing app-based drivers to stay independent contractors but guaranteeing them some benefits, like a healthcare subsidy and pay for their time driving engaged. Uber’s CEO, Dara Khosrowshahi, among others, applauded the law for offering flexibility. Others saw it as a way for profitable tech companies to escape the burden of employing workers.

So in 2020, Uber drivers were faced with a choice between freedom and exploitation. The app gave them some control over their hours, but not control over their rates, their costs, their health, or their benefits. Freedom would be for Uber drivers to be able to keep deciding their hours while also having more protections from illness, accidents, and income volatility. In 2020, the big lesson was that freedom isn’t much if workers have to take nearly all the risks while companies keep most of the power.

Toni Morrison shows in Beloved (1987) that the pain of slavery does not fade with the abolition of it; it lives on in memory, a ghost that haunts the present as the ghost in 124 Bluestone Road. The fugitive slave Sethe, living in Cincinnati in 1873, eighteen years after she fled from Sweet Home plantation in Kentucky, is unable to shake off the constant return of her "rememory." Morrison's coinage of the term implies that memories are not personal property, but possessive powers that are held in the world, waiting to jump out and surprise you. Sethe cautions her daughter Denver that even if you forget the humiliation of Sweet Home, "it's still out there." You can experience the past there still.

The pivotal horror of the novel - the murder of her two-year-old daughter in 1855 to keep her from being returned to slavery - is intentionally withheld from the reader and shown piecemeal, just as trauma memories work. Sethe cannot and therefore does not provide a straightforward narrative of the event; it keeps coming back in bits and pieces, set off by sensory stimuli. In the bodily appearance of Beloved at 124, seemingly the daughter come back from the dead at the age she should be, around nineteen, Morrison makes literal the intransigence of the past that will not be buried. The past in the form of Beloved absorbs the tales of Sethe and wants to hear them over and over again. The teller almost dies from the telling and remembering.

At the same time, Morrison argues for the essential, painful necessity of memory. The neglect of Sethe by the community (symbolized by the forgotten sermons of Baby Suggs in the Clearing) allows the ghost to grow. It is only when thirty women come to 124 to sing and pray that Beloved can be banished. Paul D's final understanding that Sethe's love was "too thick" and his pledge to massage her feet imply that the solution is to share and remember, not to be alone. With the dedication of the book to "Sixty Million and more," Morrison makes clear that Sethe's story represents a collective one that had been silenced. In giving narrative life to the unsayable, Morrison argues that people cannot progress until they face what happened and that literature can be a way to remember. Beloved ends with a paradox in the cautioning "This is not a story to pass on." It is at once a story not to be repeated, but also not to be let go or forgotten or overlooked.

In her novel Beloved (1987), Toni Morrison shows how the horrors of slavery do not end with freedom; they live on in the memory like the ghost of 124 Bluestone Road. In 1873, eighteen years after escaping the Sweet Home plantation in Kentucky, Sethe, the escaped slave in Cincinnati, is still haunted by what she calls "rememory." As Morrison coins this term, memory is not an object in Sethe's possession but a presence, a repository of the world waiting to spring its trap on anyone who crosses its path. Even if she forgets the disgrace of Sweet Home, Sethe warns her daughter Denver, "it's still out there." It is still a place where the past can happen to you.

The ultimate outrage in Beloved-Sethe's murder of her two-year-old daughter in 1855 to spare her from returning to slavery-is purposefully not told to the reader outright, but told piecemeal in the manner that trauma actually works in memory. Sethe cannot tell the story straight and so she doesn't; it comes in pieces when Sethe's memories are triggered by details. In the physical appearance of Beloved at 124, as if Sethe's dead child has returned to the age she would be, around nineteen, Morrison makes her point of how the past will not be laid to rest. Beloved gorges on Sethe's tales, beseeching her to tell and retell until the very telling and remembering nearly drive the teller mad.

However, Morrison stresses the importance of memory, no matter how painful. The forgetting of the community, as represented by Baby Suggs's forsaken sermons in the Clearing, helps the ghost to thrive. Only when thirty women come to 124 to sing and pray is Beloved exorcized. In his final revelation that Sethe's love was "too thick" and in his pledge to rub her feet, Paul D provides a clue that it is in collective remembering, not in aloneness, that healing can take place. Dedicating the novel to "Sixty Million and more," Morrison reveals that Sethe's story represents a shared history that had been silenced. In giving narrative form to the inexpressible, Morrison makes her point that it is necessary for a people to look at what has happened before they can go forward, and that literature can be itself a remembering. At the end of Beloved, she warns, "This is not a story to pass on," but this paradox of a statement could be saying the story must not be repeated and also that it must not be passed over, forgotten or ignored.

the acetone / nail polish remover smell is normal for young starter, it's actually a sign that it's fermenting! not dying! 
 What's going on:  Wild yeast + bacteria in your flour are starting to produce acetic acids + esters after 48-72 hours or so as they eat up the starches. When your starter starts getting hungry (lacking new food between feedings) it starts cycling through different bacterial activity that makes acetone-y smelling stuff. (this is especially likely if you're using whole grain flour (rye, whole wheat) vs all purpose - because it'll ferment more quickly and strongly) 
 How to deal: 
 1. Feed more often! For 3-4 days, feed every 12 hours instead of 24. 1:1:1 weight (50g starter, 50g flour, 50g water @78F or so) 
 2. Make sure you're balancing flour/water ratios right - if your starter's too liquidy, the acids are building up quicker. Thicker (same weight) will slow it down. 
 3. Keep your temp constant - if your counter is over 75F (like, next to an oven or in a really hot kitchen) the fermentation is speeding up and using up food faster. Try to keep it around 68-75F  (I had mine next to the coffee maker away from the stove and it really made a difference!) 
 You'll often notice at 4-6 days it'll start SMELLING  WORSE  (gym socks, vomit smelling stuff, various bacteria are fighting it out) before it starts smelling better! Don't throw out your hands, don't panic. By 7-10 days most will have a nice yeasty / slightly tangy / apple cider vinegar smell and will be reliably rising (doubling every 4-6 hours after feeding) 
 When to be worried: only if you notice pink / orange lines (mold) or fuzzy stuff on the top. If it's only smelling acetone-y don't toss it - you're just starving it! Feed regularly and it'll get back to normal. 
 Source: using same starter since March 2021, and it always smelled like a nail salon whenever I forgot to feed it 1 day too many.

that acetone/nail polish smell is totally fine in a young starter. it's a good thing! it's fermentation. 
 what's going on: after 48-72h the wild yeast/bacteria in your flour will start making acetic acid and esters while they're eating up the starches. as your starter starts running low on new food sources between feedings, the bacteria change what they're doing and start making acetone-y smelling stuff. this can be even worse with whole grain flours (rye, whole wheat etc) because they ferment faster/more viciously than ap. 
 
 how to help it: 
 
 feed more often: 12h instead of 24h for the next 3-4 days. 1:1:1 by weight (ex 50g starter, 50g flour, 50g water at ~78F) 
 
 make sure your flour:water ratio is ok: if it's too wet it causes acids to build up more rapidly, but if you make it slightly thicker (same wgt:wgt) it slows it down 
 
 try to keep the temperature stable: if your counter is hot (over 75F like, next to the oven or in a hot room) it'll ferment faster and burn out of its food more quickly. aim for 68-75F. i keep mine next to the coffee maker (far from the stove) and it was a game changer. 
 what to expect: on days 4-6 it can smell like shit (literally, like gym socks or vomit sometimes) as different kinds of bacteria fight. don't freak out. don't throw it away. by 7-10 days most starters should have a pleasant yeasty/tangy (apples cider vinegar-y smell) with good rising power (it should double in 4-6h from feeding) 
 only throw it away if you see pink or orange (mold) or fluffy stuff on top. acetone smell does not mean 'throw it away', your starter just has the munchies. keep feeding it regularly and it'll be fine. 
 Source: I've had the same starter since march 2021 and every time I forgot to feed it for too long it would smell like the nail salon.

datetime.utcnow() (and utcfromtimestamp()) **deliberately** produce a naive datetime object. It'll return you UTC wallclock times, but it'll remove the tzinfo so that no indication of UTC appears on the object.

That's why it's been deprecated in Python 3.12! Because it's so easy to take that naive datetime, think it's local time, then get non-obvious incorrect results if you compare it to an aware datetime or convert it to another timezone with astimezone().

Just don't use utcnow() anymore and make a datetime with tzinfo instead:

```
import datetime
from datetime import datetime, timezone

now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
```

This `now` will have tzinfo=timezone.utc. So now.isoformat() will give you e.g. "2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983+00:00" not just "2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983" which can be anything.

(3.11+ can use datetime.UTC as a shortcut for timezone.utc.)

Other things you'll want to do in 2024+ code:

* Don't mix naive and aware datetime objects in comparisons. Python will raise TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes (which is good), but you must be consistent.
* If you want more than just UTC, like e.g. America/Chicago or Asia/Tokyo, don't use pytz, use the standard library zoneinfo module (3.9+):

```
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
chicago = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("America/Chicago"))
```

* Store your timestamps as UTC (aware or explicitly UTC-naive but consistent) in your database. Only convert to your local zone at the display level.

* If you're using Django, USE_TZ=True and django.utils.timezone.now() will already be doing the right thing and following this approach.

Anyway: datetime.now(timezone.utc) is the straight-up replacement (non-deprecated) for datetime.utcnow().

And that's why it's deprecated in Python 3.12, because it's quite easy to do stuff like take that naive object and just assume it's in localtime and wind up with completely wrong results by comparing it to an aware datetime, or converting it with astimezone().

The solution is to avoid using utcnow() altogether, and instead create an aware datetime:

now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

That `now` object will have tzinfo set to timezone.utc so the call to `now.isoformat()` will end up printing the full thing with 2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983+00:00 rather than just 2026-09-21T14:32:07.512983 (which could be anything). You can also use datetime.UTC as a shortcut for timezone.utc if you're on Python 3.11+.

Oh, some other things to do in 2024 code:

- avoid having naive and aware datetimes in your code together for comparisons; Python will give you TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes, and that's great (because it stops you from doing things silently wrong), but you need to be consistent everywhere.
- avoid using naive datetimes in your code for more than just UTC (i.e. if you want America/Chicago or Asia/Tokyo, etc.), and use the stdlib's zoneinfo module (3.9+) instead of pytz;
  from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
  chicago = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("America/Chicago"))
- store the timestamps in your DB as UTC (either aware or explicitly UTC-naive, be consistent), and only convert to a local timezone in the display layer.

So, datetime.now(timezone.utc) is a direct (and non-deprecated!) replacement for datetime.utcnow().

As a freelancer, I would advise you to build 6-12 months worth of critical personal expenses, not a specific dollar amount. It's more relevant to have the higher number when your income isn't consistent, instead of the typical 3 months we're usually told to shoot for.

Example: If you're based in Portland, Oregon and your minimum monthly expenses are:

Rent/utilities: $1,800 
 Health insurance/medical expenses: $500 
 Food: $500 
 Transportation: $250 
 Minimum debt payments/other critical expenses: $150 

Your critical monthly costs are $3,200. A reasonable amount for your emergency fund might be $19,200 to cover 6 months, but $28,800 would be a nice, 9-month buffer.

Set up 3 separate accounts for:

1. Emergencies: Job loss, sickness, big surprise expenses
2. Taxes: Savings for federal/state quarterly tax estimates
3. Business: Software, equipment replacement, subcontractors, slow paying clients

Otherwise, a huge tax bill and a broken laptop might make your "emergency fund" look bigger than it really is.

Use your minimum reasonable monthly spending, not your average lifestyle, to figure out the goal. Regularly pay yourself from your business account, say $4,000 a month, and put any months where you did really well into savings. Rebuild your emergency fund after you tap into it. And keep it in an easy-to-get-to savings account that's FDIC insured. Don't use investments.

The CFPB specifically says that emergency funds are helpful for those with inconsistent income. The FDIC recommends 3-6 months (in general) and that those with very uncertain employment may need to plan for 6+ months. [CFPB advice](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/an-essential-guide-to-building-an-emergency-fund/) and [FDIC advice](https://www.fdic.gov/consumer-resource-center/2025-01/saving-unexpected-and-your-future).

You should be paying yourself a consistent amount -- let's say $4k/month -- out of your business account.  And squirreling away when things are especially good.  And replacing the emergency fund when you use it.  And don't invest this -- just put it in a convenient savings account, in FDIC-insured form. 
 Note that the CFPB specifically mentions emergency funds as helpful for those who have sporadic income.  The FDIC mentions 3-6 months as a general rule, but also that those who are unusually uncertain about employment should be thinking about 6 months or more. Could be a number of things, but as the grinding is happening on a 2009 civic here are the most likely things: 
 Most likely you just have worn out brake pads. Civics from that generation (06-11) tend to wear out the front brake pads somewhere between 40-60k miles. If they are down to the backing plate (metal) you will hear grinding and the sound is often worse going downhill because you are under more aggressive/longer braking so more heat and pressure. If you are hearing grinding when you apply the brakes then this is your first suspect. Remove a wheel or look through the holes and you should see the brake pad friction material should be at least 3mm thick. If you see grooves or scoring on the rotor face then you've been riding the pads on the metal for a while and you need rotors too. Expect ~$150-$250 an axle (pads and rotors) from an independent shop. 
 Why when going downhill?  Couple reasons: 
 1. Heat.  If you are doing extended braking downhill (like going down a long hill) then you are generating heat on the rotors. If they are warped or have deposits you will feel a pulsing and sometimes hear groaning/grinding. Warped rotors are fairly common if brake pads were neglected at some point in the cars life. 
 2. Weight transfer.  When you are braking downhill more weight is on the front brakes so you may hear noise from worn pads/rotors more. 
 Other possible things: 
 - Glazed brake pads. If your PO was a brakes rider then their pads could glaze and get hard and you will hear a grind/growl under braking pressure. 
 - Stuck caliper. On 8th gen civics it isn't uncommon to have a frozen caliper slide pin. It will drag on the pad and the rotor and cause a grinding noise especially when hot. See if one of the wheels is dustier or hotter than the rest after driving. 
 - Rust on rotors.  If the car sits for many days rust will form on the rotors and cause noise. This usually goes away after a few stops but if it's grinding constantly it's not that. 
 Don't wait. Grinding means metal to metal. The longer you wait the more you will be eating up rotors and it could lead to a ruined caliper. If you're handy it's very much doable to replace brake pads and rotors on a civic as a DIY project. Maybe 2 hours with basic tools. If not get it in this week. 
 Try this:  does it only grind when you apply the brakes? Or does it also do it when you coast downhill with your foot off the pedal? If it also does it when coasting it could be a wheel bearing or stuck caliper. Not the pads. This will give your mechanic a lot of information.

 If you're a W-2 employee (as implies by "working remotely for my employer") then the miscellaneous itemized deduction (including the home office deduction) for unreimbursed employee business expenses is suspended for 2018-2025 under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. So whether you work from home 1 day per week or 5 days per week, if you're a W-2 employee, you can't take it on your federal return, period.  State taxes. Some states (CA, NY, PA, AL, AR) let you take the unreimbursed employee expenses deduction on the state return even though it's suspended at the federal level. Check the rules for your particular state in 2025.

2 in hole? Instead of trying to fill the hole with just joint compound. Use a self adhesive metal patch (drywall) for the hole.

First cut away any loose paper. Then use a utility knife to cut the ragged edges square. Blow off any dust. Then place a 4 in or bigger metal mesh patch over the center of the hole. Press down on the patch to make it flat. If the hole is near a corner or a stud. Then make sure the patch doesn't go over any uneven surface.

Next, put setting type joint compound over the patch. Such as 45 minute Easy Sand. Using a 6 in taping knife. Feather the compound out at least 3 in on all sides of the patch. Allow the patch to set up. Then remove any ridges by scraping. Put on a second coat of joint compound but make it thinner. Then you may need to add a skim coat for a 3rd time to completely cover the patch.

Once the last coat has set (usually overnight). Then lightly sand using 150 or 220 grit sandpaper. Now if you can feel a ridge when you run your hand over the patch. Do not sand the patch hard. Instead add more compound. Wipe away any dust. Then prime the patch using drywall primer. Then paint to match the wall color.

Since it is a door knob. You will want to add a door stop or a hinge pin stop after you repair the door knob. If you have a door knob that hits the wall. Then a rubber stop that mounts to the wall is usually the best. If the hole is near an electrical outlet or switch. Then turn off the circuit before you cut or sand. And do not drive screws near that area.

For a 2-in. hole, don't try to fill it with drywall joint compound. Instead, get a self-adhesive metal drywall patch.

Cut away any torn paper. Smooth out any rough edges with a utility knife. Wipe away dust. Center a metal mesh patch (4 in. or larger) over the hole. Press it firmly to flatten it out. Don't use the patch over a bump if the damage is near a corner or stud.

Spread setting-type joint compound (like 45-minute Easy Sand) over the patch. Use a 6-in. taping knife and feather out the compound at least 3 in. from the patch. Allow it to set up. Scrape away ridges. Apply a second coat that's thinner. You may need to apply a third skim coat to completely conceal the patch.

Sand gently (with 150- or 220-grit sandpaper) after the last coat dries (usually overnight). If you can feel a ridge when you run your hand across the repair, don't sand hard. Add more joint compound instead. Wipe away dust, prime the repair with drywall primer, and paint with the same wall color.

Since the hole was made by a door knob, you should add a doorstop or a hinge pin stop after making the repair. If you have a door knob that is hitting the wall, you probably want a rubber stop on the wall. If your hole is near an electrical outlet or switch, turn off the circuit before cutting or sanding, and don't put any screws in that area.

Well, great news. 120/80 at age 55 is a pretty healthy reading. Actually, it's the 'ideal' according to the textbooks. 
 The American Heart Association says a reading below 120/80 is 'normal' and 120-129 sys/less than 80 dia is 'elevated.' Stage 1 HTN kicks in at 130/80. Stage 2 at 140/90. So you're basically at the upper limit of the normal range, which is where a lot of healthy 55 year-olds will be. With age and hardening of the arteries, blood pressure tends to rise, so if you're in your mid-50s and sitting at 120/80, that's a good sign (not a bad sign). 
 Some caveats: 
 1. Don't make a diagnosis from one reading. Blood pressure can fluctuate with time of day, stress, caffeine, sleep, talking during the reading, etc. If your 120/80 was from just one reading at a pharmacy machine or a stressful doctor visit, try to take a few more at home (sitting down, supported arm, five minute rest) for a week or two. See what the average is. 
 2. Don't just look at the number. When you're 55, your doc should also be looking at your cholesterol, glucose levels, family history, smoking, weight, etc. Your blood pressure might be fine, but you might have elevated risk for other reasons. 
 3. Monitor it. Guidelines say to check it at least once a year at your physical or check it more often if there's a family history of HTN. 
 Moderate salt intake (less than 2300mg/day. ideally less than 1500mg/day), aerobic exercise (at least 150 mins/week), cut back on alcohol, maintain a healthy weight. You know the drill. 
 So no, don't worry. It's a number most 55 year-olds would like to have. But do mention it next time you go for a checkup and monitor it over time -- that's what's more important than a single number. 
 *standard disclaimer: I'm not a doctor. If you're having symptoms (headaches, dizzy, chest pain, etc.), go see your doc regardless of your numbers*

The surefire solution is baking soda paste, takes about 10 minutes:
 - 3 baking soda to 1 water to form paste (something like 3 tbsp to 1 tbsp for normal 18" board)
 - rub paste into board with a clean cloth or cut end of a lemon half, with the grain, and let sit 5-10 minutes
 - rinse with hot water and wipe dry immediately, on its edge so it doesn't warp
 
If the odor persists, use coarse salt for a mechanical action. Just spread a layer on the board, then scrub with a half of lemon. Use the salt as a medium to remove. The citric acid in the lemon will break down the sulfur compounds in the garlic which "stick" (same allicin breakdown products that cause garlic breath), and the salt will act as a medium to pull out of the wood grain. Rinse and wipe dry. 
 
If you have a board with months of garlic/onion odor absorption, you can try a deeper soak. Put 1 tbsp baking soda in a quart of warm water and let the board soak in (or covered in paste) for 15-20 minutes, then scrub with a stiff brush against the grain. 
 
Don't do:
 - Don't put a wood board through a dishwasher, or soak it for hours. For end grain boards especially it will cause cracking or delamination. 
 - Don't initially try vinegar by itself. It can soften the natural oils in the wood through repeated application. You can use it sometimes, 1:1 with water and quickly wipe and rinse. 
 - After wiping dry, wipe a mineral oil (food safe) or board cream (mixture of beeswax and mineral oil) into the board. This reconditions it and will also make it smell less, next time, since a more oiled board is less porous. 
 
If you cut lots of garlic, consider having a separate little board for your "pungent" foods, so you never get stuck with this on your main board.

If you have a table called `users` with a column called `email`:
- group by the email, retaining any groups which have more than one row in:
```sql
SELECT
  email,
  COUNT(*) AS duplicate_count
FROM users
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY email
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY duplicate_count DESC, email;
```
That will give you a list of each duplicate email and how many copies there are. So if there's 3 copies of alex@example.com then it will show:
 alex@example.com | 3

If you want to regard multiple email addresses as duplicates no matter whether there are spaces around them or they are mixed-case:
 - normalise the emails in the query:
```sql
SELECT
  LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalized_email,
  COUNT(*) AS duplicate_count
FROM users
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY duplicate_count DESC;
```

If you want to see the actual users rows:
- use a derived table:
```sql
SELECT u.*
FROM users AS u
  JOIN
    ( SELECT
        LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalized_email
      FROM users
      WHERE email IS NOT NULL
      GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
        HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
    ) AS d ON LOWER(TRIM(u.email)) = d.normalized_email
ORDER BY d.normalized_email, u.id;
```

That's still a regular aggregate query even though you have 2 million rows. You can speed it up a bit by adding an index. Assuming you have an appropriate one, add an index on the normalised value:
 eg for postgreSQL:
```sql
CREATE INDEX users_email_normalized_idx ON
  users (LOWER(TRIM(email)));
```

If you don't want them to be duplicated in future then you can constrain against it, for example if you're using postgreSQL:
```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_unique_idx ON
  users (LOWER(TRIM(email)))
  WHERE email IS NOT NULL;
```

Make sure you deal with (or decide what to do about) any existing duplicates before you do this, since it's going to fail trying to create the index while there are duplicate normalised email addresses.

 COUNT(*) as duplicate_count
FROM users
 WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
 ORDER BY duplicate_count DESC;

Now you need to get actual users that have these duplicates.

SELECT u.*
FROM users as u
 JOIN (
 SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) as normalized_email
 FROM users
 WHERE email IS NOT NULL
 GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
 ) as d
 ON LOWER(TRIM(u.email)) = d.normalized_email
 ORDER BY d.normalized_email, u.id;

This is still a normal aggregation query even for 2 mln rows but you can speed it up with index. Make index on normalized value, if your DB supports it. (PostgreSQL, e.g.)

CREATE INDEX users_email_normalized_idx
ON users(LOWER(TRIM(email)));

Enforce uniqueness for future inserts if you don't want duplicate emails. (PostgreSQL again)

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_unique_idx
ON users(LOWER(TRIM(email)))
WHERE email IS NOT NULL;

But clean/decide what to do with them first since creating that index will fail as long as there are duplicate normalized emails.

MEMORANDUM
 To: Maria Delgado, Chief Financial Officer
 From: James Okonkwo, Chief Information Security Officer
 Date: March 14, 2025
 Re: FY2026 Cybersecurity Budget Request - From $4.2M to $4.7M

Purpose
 I am seeking a 12% increase in our FY2026 budget for the Cybersecurity Department, moving from $4.2 million to $4.7 million. This memo outlines the rationale, budget breakdown, and anticipated benefits.

Rationale
 The increase is justified by:

1. Compliance Requirements: We need to enhance monitoring and documentation for audit preparations (SOC 2 Type II) and the new state privacy law taking effect on January 1, 2026. (Approx. incremental compliance cost: $180,000)

2. Threat Landscape: In FY2025, we've seen 14 targeted phishing attacks (vs. 6 in previous year) and two close calls with ransomware (Q3 2025). Our SIEM licensing and 24/7 monitoring contract (SentinelWatch) will expire in August 2025 and need renewal at 9% increased cost.

3. Business Expansion: As we open Denver in October 2025 and grow to 850 employees, our attack surface has increased by ~20% since FY2024 budget planning.

Proposed Distribution of $500K Increase
 - SIEM renewal and extended monitoring: $220,000
 - Extra security engineer (1 FTE, fully costed): $165,000
 - Multi-factor authentication enhancement and endpoint detection tools: $75,000
 - Employee security training program (across offices): $40,000

Options Considered
 We can't delay the SIEM renewal - gaps would breach cyber insurance terms and leave us potentially liable for $2M (uninsured). We considered outsourced engineering (managed services were 30% more expensive than internal hire over 3 years).

Anticipated Benefits
 The investment should allow us to: Be fully audit compliant by Q2 FY2026 Reduce detection time from 6 hrs to <90 minutes Complete zero trust implementation by June 2026

I can discuss further at your convenience. I can also present to the Finance Committee on April 22 if needed.

MEMORANDUM

To: All Employees From: Dana Whitfield VP Human Resources Date: November 14, 2024 Subject: Update to Parental Leave Policy (effective January 1, 2025)

I'm writing today to inform you that as the result of a competitive benefits benchmarking analysis performed this fall, we have decided to increase our paid parental leave from 8 weeks to 16 weeks effective January 1, 2025.

In Q3, HR conducted a benchmark analysis of paid parental leave benefit offered by 12 peer companies within our industry, including our three top talent competitors. The median paid parental leave benefit of our peer group was 14 weeks and many companies had recently extended their benefit to 16 weeks or more. Previously, we had an 8-week benefit, putting us in the bottom quartile. In the past 18 months, according to recruiting exit surveys, this was a reason for declined offers in 23% of cases.

Background

Effective January 1, 2025, we will provide 16 weeks of paid parental leave (vs. 8 weeks) to all eligible full-time employees when they become parents by birth, adoption, or foster placement. This includes:

• Leave is limited to 12 months from the child's arrival • All parents, regardless of gender and caregiving role, are eligible • Can be taken all at once or in two segments (if approved by manager) • For employees who started their leave on/after October 1, 2024, if you want to take additional leave under this policy, please reach out to HR to extend your leave period

Employees will still be covered for job protection under the FMLA and state laws. Our policy will be more generous than both.

We are NOT changing

Our current short-term disability benefits (up to 8 weeks provided by Lincoln Financial for birth mothers) will still apply and run concurrent with the first weeks of parental leave. Our current 4 weeks of paid caregiver leave (when there is a family medical emergency) will remain the same.

Cost

We estimate the cost of this increased benefit to be $740K annually. The Finance Committee approved this cost as part of the FY2025 benefits budget on November 6. We expect to see some savings in turnover, which in our 2023 analysis we found cost on average 42% of an employee's salary to replace them.

Please send any questions to hr@company.com or we can discuss on Dec 3 (all hands meeting). Updated policy will be available on the HR portal by December 15.

Summary We recommend termination of the Centerville retail store upon lease expiration (Aug 31, 2025). The store remains uneconomic despite consistent management oversight, cost management, and attempts to increase sales. The operating losses are impacting other, more profitable stores and preventing investment in e-commerce, customer retention, and profitable geographies.

Over the last 12 months, the Centerville store has produced ~ $1.2M in sales, but ~ $1.45M in operating costs - for a $250K estimated annual loss. The store's average sales per month are down ~8% year-on-year. Rent, labor, utilities and inventory costs are up. Customer traffic is well below the volume needed to sustain the store's current size.

Terminating the store upon lease expiration avoids renewing the lease, saves fixed operating costs, and avoids ~$150K in scheduled facility and merchandising investments. We calculate the store's termination will add ~$230K to our annual operating income (after accounting for one-time costs such as severance, inventory markdowns, move costs, and lease termination).

Centerville staff should be notified with at least 60 days' time. We should offer positions to qualified staff at the Riverside and Northgate stores (if any openings exist). Inventory should be transferred to neighboring stores (and the online business) starting in June 2025. A controlled clearance should run in July and August. The customer message should be "We're still here for you (online store) and we're near you (neighboring stores)."

Formal communication to landlord should occur no later than May 31, 2025. Employee discussions should be finalized by June 15, 2025. The store should be shut down at the end of business Aug 31, 2025. This is the financially responsible, operationally feasible, and strategic move to focus resources on our more profitable channels and stores.

We suggest termination of the lease (expiration 8/31/2025) at the Centerville retail store. Despite ongoing management focus, expense management, and sales enhancement initiatives, the Centerville location has never been profitable. The operational losses at the store are causing distraction from better performing locations and preventing investment in e-commerce, customer retention and profitable markets.

Sales at the Centerville location were approximately $1.2 million over the past 12 months. However, operating expenses for the same period were approximately $1.45 million resulting in an estimated annual loss of $250,000. Average monthly sales at the store are down about 8% on a year over year basis. Also, monthly rent, labor, utilities and inventory carry charges have increased. Additionally, customer traffic at the store is well below sustainable levels for the size of the store.

To avoid lease renewal costs, cut fixed operating costs, and eliminate the roughly $150,000 capital (facility and merchandising) investment currently planned, we suggest terminating the location at lease expiration. The estimated annual increase in operating income as a result of the closure (after one time costs such as severance, inventory markdown, relocation and lease termination activities) is approximately $230,000.

We suggest a minimum of 60 day notification to Centerville store employees, and a transfer for qualified employees to the Riverside and Northgate stores (where positions are available). We suggest inventory re-allocation to adjacent stores and the company's online store to start in June of 2025. This would be followed up with a controlled clearance process in July and August of 2025. We suggest emphasizing in communications to customers continued service through our online store and surrounding locations.

We suggest formal notification to the landlord by May 31, 2025 (no later). Consultations with employees by June 15. Closure of the store at the close of business August 31, 2025. This is a sound business decision, operationally feasible, and supports the company's strategy of focusing investment in profitable channels and locations.

TO: Executive Leadership Team
FROM: Human Resources - Total Rewards
DATE: September 21, 2026
SUBJECT: Voluntary (Pre-Dec. 2026) Phased Retirement Program for Employees 60+

We are recommending the implementation of a voluntary Phased Retirement Program beginning November 1, 2026, with 85 (currently eligible) employees age 60+ completing the phased transition by December 31, 2026.

Background/Rationale: Based on our work-force analysis, we have 85 employees who are eligible for a Phased Retirement Program (Mfg - 34, Finance/Acctg - 19, IT - 17, Corporate Admin - 15) at our Dayton, OH and Charlotte, NC sites (age 60+ and 10+ years of service). The primary motivation for the program is to preserve institutional knowledge, but also to control succession risk and manage payroll expenses.

Program Elements: Employees who are eligible and choose to participate in the Phased Retirement Program can select a 12-month transition plan that consists of working 80%/80% schedule/pay for first 4 months, 60%/60% schedule/pay for next 4 months, 40%/40% schedule/pay for last 4 months while still receiving 100% health benefits for the duration of the program and 401(k) match (on actual earnings). Participants formally separate from the company at the end of 12 months or at their own selected retirement date, whichever comes first.

Financial Implications: The approximate net payroll savings are $2.1M for FY2027, offset by a one-time stipend for knowledge transfer/mentoring ($180,000) (i.e., $2,100 for enrolled participants - up to 60 participants). Based on our research into peer companies' similar programs, we anticipate that 60-65 of our 85 eligible employees will participate.

Compliance: The program will be strictly voluntary (opt-in basis) to adhere to the Older Workers Benefit Protection Act (OWBPA) and ADEA. No employees will be coerced or forced to participate in this program. We will work with Legal (contact: General Counsel's Office) to ensure any communications are approved prior to distribution. When (if) a release of claims is requested as part of the enrollment process, the typical considerations period (45-days) and revocation period (7-days) will be in effect.

Schedule:
Oct. 5, 2026: Legal review completed
Oct. 19, 2026: Manager presentations
Nov. 1, 2026: Enrollment Period Opens (Enrollment Period ends Nov. 30, 2026)
Dec. 2026: Start transition for employees who elect to participate

We are seeking approval to move forward with the Legal review by September 30, 2026.

paper_section_01_luna.text:
Following the 2020 CASP14 evaluation, AlphaFold2 was released and appeared in Nature in 2021. AlphaFold2 was a major breakthrough in protein structure prediction, featuring the Evoformer network, which recurrently exchanged data between multiple sequence alignments (MSA) and residue pairs with attention and outer product operations. A structure module, leveraging invariant point attention (IPA), mapped these data to 3D space. Through the fusion of sequence evolution and geometric reasoning, as well as iterative refinement, AlphaFold2 reached the median GDT-TS score of 92.4 in CASP14, including the median score of 87.0 for challenging free-modeling targets. In particular, IPA was critical, its attention is applied to learned 3D points and invariant to global rotations and translations. [Jumper et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2)

Alternative methods then extended these attention-driven approaches. RoseTTAFold by University of Washington and appearing in Science in 2021 built a network with three tracks for the simultaneous modelling of 1D sequence/MSA, 2D residue pair and 3D coordinate features. Attention, graph-transformer, and SE(3) equivariant layers enabled a flow of information between these representations, with end-to-end computations on an RTX 2080 GPU predicting backbone coordinates in about 10 minutes for proteins under 400 residues. [Baek et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj8754) Meanwhile, protein language models shifted structure prediction to a natural result of sequence-level representation learning. Meta's ESM-2 and ESMFold exploited embeddings derived from Transformer language models to predict protein structures from single sequences, bypassing MSA calculations. Appearing in Science in 2023, ESMFold powered the ESM Metagenomic Atlas with over 617 million predictions, though its accuracy often lagged behind AlphaFold2. [Lin et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ade2574)

More recently, AlphaFold3 appeared in Nature in 2024, representing a leap from protein folding to biomolecular interaction modelling. It substituted the AlphaFold2 IPA structure module with a diffusion-based generative model, extending to protein-nucleic acid-ligand-ion-modified-residue modelling. In this way, transformer-driven protein prediction has shifted from geometric attention given MSA inputs to multimodal foundation models integrating language, equivariant geometry, and diffusion coordinate generation.

The release of AlphaFold2 (post-2020 CASP14 assessment, Nature, 2021) was a landmark shift in protein structure prediction. It implemented a series of swaps between multi-sequence-alignment (MSA)-conditioned and residue-pair representations using attention and outer product updates with the Evoformer. These representations were mapped to 3D coordinates using a structure module using invariant point attention (IPA). Through the integration of sequence evolution and geometric inference, as well as recycle prediction, AlphaFold2 delivered a median GDT-TS of 92.4 in CASP14, including a median value of 87.0 on the challenging free-modeling targets. The IPA module was key because it implemented attention over learned 3D points with invariance to global rotations and translations. (Jumper et al., 2021) 10.1038/s41586-021-03819-2

Following architectures then expanded on this attention-based approach. The RoseTTAFold architecture (University of Washington, Science, 2021) implemented a 3-track approach with parallel information flow across 1D sequence/MSA, 2D residue-pair, and 3D coordinate information. Attention, graph transformer and SE(3)-equivariant layers enable interchange between representations, and an end-to-end system for proteins less than 400 residues achieved backbone coordinate generation in ~10 min on RTX 2080 GPU. (Baek et al., 2021) 10.1126/science.abj8754

At the same time, protein language models positioned structure prediction as an emergent property of language-scale sequence representation. Models like ESM-2 and ESMFold (Meta) used transformer-based language model embeddings for single-sequence structure prediction, bypassing the computational overhead of explicit MSAs. The ESMFold model (Science, 2023) powered the ESM Metagenomic Atlas of structure predictions for over 617 million proteins, with generally lower accuracy than AlphaFold2. (Lin et al., 2023) 10.1126/science.ade2574

Finally, in 2024 AlphaFold3 was released in Nature. This further expanded the shift from protein folding to biomolecular interactions by abandoning the IPA structure module of AlphaFold2 for a diffusion-based generative approach that can model proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, ions, and modified residues together. Overall, protein transformer prediction has shifted from MSA-conditioned geometric attention to multimodal foundation models of language, equivariant geometric, and diffusion-based coordinate generation.

Results
The addition of CsBr to the perovskite precursor solution (MAPbI3 methylammonium lead iodide) resulted in a significant increase in PCE. The PCE of the champion devices with 5 mol% CsBr addition was 19.4%, compared to 18.1% for undoped devices (control), representing a 7.2% increase in relative yield (1.3% absolute). The same effect was observed on three different device production batches performed from March to May 2024, and the PCE of the champion devices was 19.1%-19.6% for the doped devices and 17.8%-18.3% for the control.

The J-V measurements of the efficiency improvement under AM 1.5G (100 mW cm −2) indicated that the main effect was a rise in the open-circuit voltage (VOC): VOC = 1.12 ± 0.02 V for the doped devices and VOC = 1.06 ± 0.03 V for the controls (n = 24 for each sample, p < 0.001, two-tailed t-test). The short-circuit current density (JSC) was slightly higher in the doped devices (JSC = 22.9 ± 0.5 mA cm −2), compared to 22.4 ± 0.6 mA cm −2 in the controls, but the fill factor (FF) was not significantly changed (FF = 0.74 ± 0.02 for both cases). The hysteresis factor was lower for the doped devices (8.3%-4.1%) due to lower ion migration by the addition of CsBr.

From the XRD analysis of the doped perovskite films, it was found that the (110) peak was shifted by 0.14° to higher 2θ values and that the PbI2 peak disappeared at 12.7°, suggesting that the A site was partially occupied by Cs + and that the phase purity increased. The SEM images show that the size of the grains increased (average size 412 ± 95 nm for the doped devices and 287 ± 78 nm for the controls) and that this was correlated with a decrease in trap states as determined by the space-charge-limited current (from 1.8 × 10 16 to 1.1 × 10 16 cm −3).

When the doped and control devices were tested under illumination (continuous lighting at 65 °C), 88% of the initial PCE was observed after 500 h for the doped devices and 74% for the controls. For higher doping levels (>5 mol% CsBr, we investigated 10 and 15 mol% doping), phase separation was observed and the performance decreased (PCE = 17.2% and 15.9%, respectively). Therefore, the 5 mol% CsBr addition was determined to be the best in the investigated composition range.

Results The incorporation of cesium bromide (CsBr) into the precursor solution of methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI 3 ) perovskite resulted in a statistically significant increase in power conversion efficiency (PCE). For 5 mol% CsBr-doped devices, a champion device PCE of 19.4% was obtained, representing a relative yield gain of 7.2% (absolute gain 1.3 percentage points) over undoped controls (PCE 18.1%). This effect was confirmed for three different batches of perovskite fabrication performed in March-May 2024, with 19.1-19.6% champion device PCE for CsBr-doped samples, compared to 17.8-18.3% for controls. Current density-voltage (J-V) characterization under AM 1.5G illumination (100 mW cm −2) indicated that the main contribution to efficiency improvement was an increase in open-circuit voltage (V OC): 1.12 ± 0.02 V for doped vs. 1.06 ± 0.03 V for controls (n = 24 for both groups, p < 0.001, two-tailed t-test). Short-circuit current density (J SC) increased slightly from 22.4 ± 0.6 to 22.9 ± 0.5 mA cm −2, while fill factor remained statistically the same (FF 0.74 ± 0.02 for both groups). Hysteresis indices fell from 8.3% to 4.1% following CsBr addition, suggesting reduced ion migration.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of the doped thin films showed that the (110) peak was shifted to a higher 2θ by 0.14°, while the PbI 2 peak at 12.7° disappeared, indicating partial replacement of Cs + into the A-site and enhanced phase purity. Scanning electron microscopy revealed larger grains (412 ± 95 nm average grain size for doped films vs. 287 ± 78 nm for controls), which correlated with a decrease in trap state density from 1.8 × 10 16 to 1.1 × 10 16 cm −3 when analyzed by space-charge-limited current analysis. Continuous illumination stability tests at 65 °C demonstrated that 88% of the initial PCE was maintained after 500 h for the doped devices compared to 74% for the controls. Higher doping levels (>5 mol%, investigated at 10 and 15 mol%) resulted in phase separation and lower efficiency (PCE 17.2% and 15.9%, respectively), demonstrating that 5 mol% CsBr was optimal in the compositional range considered.

Prediction of 90-day readmission to hospital using gradient boosting and longitudinal electronic health record data from MIMIC-IV

BACKGROUND: Despite the high cost and importance, 90-day readmission after discharge is poorly studied, as most prediction models focus on the more clinically relevant 30-day readmission required by CMS for reporting.

METHODS: Adult inpatients (2008-2019) with 51,238 admissions were extracted from MIMIC-IV v2.2 database (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA). After excluding in-hospital deaths and hospice discharge, 46,904 index admissions were included. A patient was readmitted at 90-days if he/she had any admission to the hospital within 90-days after discharge (positive rate 21.4%, n=10,038). We constructed 187 features from demographics, Elixhauser comorbidity scores, admission severity measures (SOFA, SAPS-II), lab trends for last 48-hours during the hospital stay, number of medications at discharge, length of stay, and number of ED visit and admission in last 12-months. We used different subject IDs to partition the dataset (70/15/15, training/validation/test) to avoid cross-contamination between different encounters. We built and compared XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost classifiers. Hyperparameter tuning was performed using 5-fold cross-validated Bayesian optimization (100 trials using Optuna) and training set, with early stopping on validation AUROC.

RESULTS: In the holdout set, LightGBM model showed the best performance (AUROC 0.762, 95%CI 0.748-0.776; AUPRC 0.451; Brier 0.142) compared to the logistic regression model (AUROC 0.681), slightly higher than XGBoost (AUROC 0.754) and CatBoost (AUROC 0.758) models. According to SHAP values, number of admission in the last 12-months, hemoglobin level at discharge, Elixhauser comorbidity score, and discharge disposition (home vs. skilled nursing facility) were the most important factors. Calibration of the LightGBM model showed a good performance in each decile risk group (Hosmer-Lemeshow p=0.34). The prediction cutoff for the top 20% of the predicted risk resulted in a sensitivity of 58.3% (i.e., rate of true readmission identified), and PPV of 47.1%.

CONCLUSIONS: Gradient boosting based on common MIMIC-IV data showed reasonable discriminative power to predict 90-day readmission risk, which may help predict patients beyond the 30-days after discharge and extend discharge planning interventions (needs external validation in the non-ICU weighted cohorts).

Prediction of 90-day hospital readmission using gradient boosting on longitudinal electronic health record data from the MIMIC-IV

Background. Unplanned hospital readmission within 90 days from discharge continues to be an important clinical endpoint and a source of significant financial loss. However, predictive models are often focused on 30-day readmissions in accordance with CMS reporting requirements and therefore longer-term risk may not be sufficiently considered.

Methods. We identified 51,238 adult inpatient encounters from MIMIC-IV v2.2 (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA) from 2008 to 2019 (excluding in-hospital deaths and hospice) for 46,904 eligible index admissions. Patients with any inpatient encounter within 90 days of discharge were considered a 90-day readmission (21.4%, n=10,038). We created 187 features including demographics, Elixhauser comorbidity, acuity scores (SOFA, SAPS-II) at admission, laboratory time series from the last 48 h of the hospital encounter, number of medications at discharge, length of stay, prior ED visit and number of inpatient admissions in the past 12 months. Patient-level encounters were separated using unique subject IDs (70/15/15 train/validate/test) to avoid temporal leakage. We constructed and evaluated XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost classifiers. We performed hyperparameter optimization using 5-fold Bayesian cross-validation (100 trials, Optuna) for the training set using a 5-fold Bayesian cross-validation with early stopping on the validation AUROC.

Results. We observed that LightGBM had the best held-out performance (AUROC 0.762 [95% CI 0.748-0.776], AUPRC 0.451, Brier score 0.142), which was better than logistic regression (AUROC 0.681), and slightly better than XGBoost (AUROC 0.754) and CatBoost (AUROC 0.758). SHAP showed that the most predictive features include past admissions in last 12 months, hemoglobin at discharge, Elixhauser comorbidity score, and disposition at discharge (skilled nursing facility vs home). There was good calibration of predicted risk over the deciles (Hosmer-Lemeshow, p=0.34). If we detect the top 20% risk using the model, we have sensitivity of 58.3% and PPV of 47.1% for readmissions.

Conclusions. Gradient boosting applied to commonly collected MIMIC-IV data can discriminate 90-day readmission risk, which is of clinical relevance and can be used to expand post-discharge planning beyond the traditional 30-day timeframe in clinical settings, if validated in a cohort not weighted for ICUs.
