In October 2023-August 2024, we randomly assigned 1,150 smallholder vegetable producers in Makueni and Kitui counties in Kenya to receive (i) information only (n = 383), (ii) information and a 50% voucher for a drip irrigation kit (n = 384), or (iii) information and a 75% voucher (n = 383). We sampled households using village-level agricultural census data. Eligible producers cultivated between 0.1 and 2.0 hectares, and rainfed or manually irrigated most of their crops. Respondents were not already using drip irrigation. We surveyed households at baseline. We stratified by baseline irrigated area within each county and randomly assigned households to one of the three treatment groups.

We held two-hour demonstrations with all treatment farmers (led by trained local agricultural extension agents) in November 2023. The demonstrations covered installation and upkeep, potential water savings, and crop-specific application rates. A demonstration plot of 0.1 hectares was used. Vouchers could be redeemed with participating agro-dealers in Makueni and Kitui through February 29, 2024. The drip kits contained a 500-liter storage tank, low-pressure filter, 100 meters of lateral tubing, and connectors. The kits were designed to irrigate at least 0.1 hectares. Information-only farmers received the same technical information without price subsidy.

Unblinded enumerators administered in-person surveys at baseline and four months after voucher expiration, and at the end of 2024's main production season. The main outcome was adoption (installing and using drip on at least 0.05 hectares in the 30 days before the endline survey). We also measured cultivated area, irrigation frequency, input spending, vegetable production, farm income, water consumption, and perceived labor needs. We measured crop production using farmer records and randomly chosen crop-cutting plots. We estimated intention-to-treat effects using ordinary least squares and included county fixed effects and pre-specified baseline controls. Standard errors were clustered at the village level.

We implemented a field experiment between October 2023 and August 2024 with 1,150 smallholder vegetable farmers in Makueni and Kitui counties, Kenya. Smallholder farms were sampled using village agricultural registers and pre-screened to ensure farmers grow 0.1-2.0 ha of land, primarily rainfed or manually irrigated, and are currently not using drip irrigation. Following the baseline survey, participants were stratified by county and baseline irrigated area, and randomly placed into one of three groups, receiving (1) information only (n = 383); (2) information and a 50% drip kit voucher (n = 384), and (3) information and a 75% drip kit voucher (n = 383).

We organized a 2 h demonstration for each household by locally trained agricultural extension agents in November 2023. Extension agents presented information on installation, maintenance, water-use reduction, and drip irrigation rates on crops, demonstrated on a 0.1 ha plot. Households holding vouchers could redeem them at selected agro-dealers in Makueni and Kitui until 29 February 2024. Drip irrigation kits consisted of a 500 L storage tank, low pressure filter, 100 m lateral lines, connectors, and sufficient to irrigate 0.1 ha of land. Information-only participants were offered the same technical advice but without any price reduction.

Trained, treatment-blinded enumerators conducted in-person surveys at baseline, 4 months after voucher expiry, and the end of 2024 main growing season. Our main outcome was drip system adoption (installation and use on at least 0.05 ha over the last 30 days before the endline survey). We also measured secondary outcomes on total area farmed, irrigation frequency, input costs, vegetable output, farm income, water demand, and perceived labor. We collected crop data using farmer records and randomly selected crop cuts. Intention-to-treat effects were calculated with ordinary least squares including county fixed effects and pre-specified baseline covariates, and clustered standard errors at the village level.

paper_section_09_glm.text:
DISCUSSION

Our 8 wk high fat diet (HFD; 60% kcal from fat) protocol produced significant and reproducible effects on murine cecal microbial composition, at the genus level, in accordance with previous literature (Bäckhed et al., 2004; Turnbaugh et al., 2006), and now in quantity with estimates of effect size and variance. Our C57BL/6J animals (n = 12 HFD and n = 11 chow control) showed strong effects on the expansion of Bilophila (14.3 fold; log2FC = 3.84; q = 0.002, adj. q value; DESeq2, Benjamini-Hochberg), whose known physiological tolerance to bile is mechanistically consistent with the rises in tauroconjugated bile acids from dietary fat intake. This result supports the hypothesized role for sulfide from Bilophila to compromise intestinal integrity.

Meanwhile, we saw a strong drop in the abundance of the mucin-active genus Akkermansia (log2FC = −2.61; q = 0.008), which has been linked to metabolic health in rodents and humans. It remains unclear whether loss of Akkermansia is a driver or biomarker of HFD-driven metabolic endotoxemia; we note here that Akkermansia loss occurred several weeks earlier than the onset of fasting glucose increase, suggesting a possible directionality, but causal effects are not concluded here.

We note that the fall in Lactobacillus (log2FC = −1.78; q = 0.03) was largely the result of 3 subjects, and sensitivity analyses with those subjects excluded were not significant (q = 0.11). Similarly, the putative increase in Clostridium XIVa (log2FC = 1.92; q = 0.048) was on the border of statistical significance and may not be indicative of increased abundance, but rather of an effect of compositional normalization, as is a limitation of relative abundance data, which we partially mitigated with the use of ANCOM-BC for additional confirmation.

HFD subjects showed a small reduction of alpha-diversity (mean Shannon index: 3.12 vs. 3.58; p-Wilcoxon = 0.009), and a separation on PCo1 of the beta-diversity (R ² PERMANOVA = 0.19; p = 0.001), suggesting that the community is perturbed by diet change in addition to individual taxa changes. We are actively investigating the question of whether these changes are reversible with return to a normal diet, as well as which taxa might predict reversal of insulin sensitivity in our lab.

Discussion

In agreement with earlier findings (Bäckhed et al., 2004;Turnbaugh et al., 2006), the 8-week high fat diet (HFD) protocol (60% kcal fat) produced marked and generally reproducible genus level changes in the murine cecal microbiome. In this study we provided quantitative insights into effect sizes and intra-individual variability. For our C57BL/6J animals (n = 12 HFD and n = 11 chow controls), the most significant change was a 14.3 fold increase (log2FC = 3.84; adj. q = 0.002, DESeq2, BH) of Bilophila, a genus whose bile tolerance phenotype has clear functional relevance in the context of increased tauro-conjugated BAs seen in the setting of fat intake. The upregulation of Bilophila supports the hypothesis that the production of sulfide by this genus may compromise the integrity of the gut barrier.

In contrast, we saw substantial loss (log2FC =-2.61, q = 0.008) of Akkermansia, a mucin degrader genus with many studies in animal models and humans linking it to metabolic function. The causality or epiphenomena of Akkermansia reduction in the context of metabolic endotoxemia resulting from HFD remains in question. Here we found that loss of Akkermansia occurred 2 weeks before significant increase in fasting glucose, suggesting potential directionality, but causality cannot be inferred from our study design.

We note two caveats. First, our reduction of Lactobacillus (log2FC =-1.78, q = 0.03) was dominated by three animals, sensitivity analysis excluding them led to a not significant effect (q = 0.11). Second, the potentially large increase of Clostridium XIVa (log2FC = 1.92, q = 0.048) approached statistical significance and could represent a compensatory effect secondary to normalization rather than a true shift, a limitation of relative abundance which we attempted to mitigate using ANCOM-BC for confirmatory analyses.

Modest reduction in alpha diversity (average Shannon index of 3.12 for HFD vs. 3.58 for controls, Wilcoxon p = 0.009), and group differentiation by beta diversity along PCo1 axis (PERMANOVA R2 = 0.19, p = 0.001) suggested the community change with the dietary challenge was not limited to individual genera. We are currently working in the lab to explore reversibility of the changes by a normalizing diet, and genera that would predict insulin sensitivity recovery.

paper_section_11_sonnet.text:
Heterogeneous treatment effects have increasingly taken center stage in labor economics, moving beyond their initial role as a robustness exercise. Bayesian approaches have emerged as particularly effective in modeling and estimating heterogeneous treatment effects under the sparse, high-dimensional contexts that are common in the context of policy evaluation. In contrast to classical methods that have difficulty reporting meaningful uncertainty for treatment effects estimated from small subgroups, Bayesian hierarchical models partially pool information across subgroups to borrow strength from the population to shrink out noisy subgroup estimates in favor of more robust population patterns. This approach was inspired by Rubin's (1981) parallels in the context of experiments and saw practical application in the context of labor economics, particularly in the context of job training programs (especially in the re-examination of National Supported Work Demonstration data that was first examined by LaLonde (1986)).

In the last decade, two recent developments have fueled greater use of these techniques. First, the recent combination of Bayesian additive regression trees (Chipman, George, and McCulloch 2010) within the context of causal inference (especially Hill's (2011) Bayesian Causal Forest) has enabled flexible nonparametric estimation of conditional average treatment effects with complete quantification of posterior uncertainty. Second, recent applications involving large datasets such as administrative data (e.g., Angrist, Pallais, et al. in the context of job-search assistance programs or datasets from Danish and German social insurance that cover populations of more than a million workers) have shown that Bayesian shrinkage can deliver considerably better performance in estimates of treatment effects with respect to unpooled subgroup estimates when treatment effects are modeled across hundreds of subgroups that may be defined along dimensions such as age, education, and local labor market conditions.

There has also been considerable literature surrounding the use of Bayesian methods to estimate instrumental variables and regression discontinuity designs, which can help resolve issues around weak instruments that have been frequently encountered in the context of the minimum wage and extended unemployment insurance. (See e.g., the Bayesian analysis of welfare-to-work experiments by Kline and Tartari (2016), as well as the meta-analysis of microcredit experiments by Meager (2019) which uses hierarchical priors to reconcile seemingly conflicting results across sites.)

This paper aims to synthesize these strands of research, comparing their relative performance in the context of simulated data that are calibrated to the labor market context in 2019 (using the Current Population Survey), and provide recommendations for empirical researchers on the choice between BART-based, Gaussian process-based, and shrinkage-prior estimators.

Bayesian statistics have been particularly helpful for estimating HT effects in the sparse and high dimensional context of policy analysis. While HT effects have gone from being a robustness exercise to the main concern in labor economics, classical inference faces problems about providing credible inference about effects among narrow groups of individuals. Bayesian hierarchical models make use of partial pooling to induce strength through cross-group similarity. Small-sample estimates from narrow subgroups are “pulled” or shrunk towards more reliable estimates from broader populations. This concept has roots in Rubin’s (1981) discussion of parallel experiments and has gained appeal through applications to job training programs in the labor economics literature, including the reanalysis of the National Supported Work Demonstration data originally analyzed by LaLonde (1986).

The recent rise of applications using Bayesian additive regression trees (Chipman, George, and McCulloch 2010) combined with causal inference (see the Bayesian Causal Forest method of Hill 2011) has provided a flexible nonparametric way to estimate conditional average treatment effects while still fully accounting for posterior uncertainty.

Finally, recent large-scale analyses of administrative data (e.g., Angrist, Pallais and co-authors’ studies of job search programs and use of Danish and German social insurance data that include more than a million workers) have shown that Bayesian shrinking greatly improves over estimates from single subgroups, especially for treatments that have effects that may vary over hundreds of groups (e.g., in age, education and labor market conditions).

Another area of literature considers the use of Bayesian models for instrumental variables and regression discontinuity designs. These studies address weak IV issues often encountered in minimum wage and UI extension research (e.g., see Bayesian studies of welfare to work programs by Kline and Tartari (2016) or meta-analysis of microcredit programs by Meager (2019), which use hierarchical priors to resolve apparently conflicting results between sites).

We survey these lines of thought and assess the relative performance in simulated labor markets (based on 2019 CPS data) to provide guidance to applied economists on the use of BARTs, Gaussian processes and shrinking priors.

paper_section_13_luna.text:
In a sample of 64 healthy infants in the University of Washington Infant Learning and Development Laboratory (Seattle, WA) during March-August 2024, infants showed a robust preference for PLW in eye-tracking data. Infants included 32 females and 32 males, ages 5-7 months (mean age = 6.1, SD = 0.7). In each trial (N = 24 trials), infants viewed either a upright PLW, inverted PLW, or phase-scrambled motion control, combined with a visually-matched display of static dots. Trials were included if infants had valid gaze tracking data for at least 50% of the 2-s trial (91.8% valid samples).

Infants spent a higher proportion of their total viewing time looking at upright PLW (M = 61.7%, 95% CI [59.2, 64.2]) compared to the visually-matched control (t(63) = 5.84, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.73). Infants showed a first fixation preference for upright PLW, which was above-chance in 68% of trials (χ2(1) = 13.76, p < .001). In contrast, infants did not reliably show an above-chance viewing preference for inverted PLW (M = 51.9%, t(63) = 1.21, p = .23) or phase-scrambled PLW (M = 49.8%, t(63) = -0.18, p = .86). A linear mixed effects model examining the influence of infant age, sex, trial type, and trial number revealed a significant effect of display type (F(2, 126) = 12.47, p < .001). Follow-up paired comparisons showed that upright PLW attracted more viewing than both inverted PLW (mean difference = 9.8 percentage points, p = .002) and scrambled (mean difference = 11.9 percentage points, p < .001). Infant age and sex did not moderate this viewing preference. These results indicate that 5-7-month-old infants can detect the meaningful, coordinated motion properties of human biological motion (rather than local dot motion or the energetic properties of the stimuli) at this age.

In 64 healthy infants (32 males; 32 females, age 5–7 months; mean age 6.1 months, SD 0.7) tested between March and August 2024 at the University of Washington Infant Learning and Development Laboratory in Seattle, eye tracking recorded a consistent preference for point light walker displays. Infants were presented with 24 trials showing an upright (or inverted) point light walker, or phase scrambled control display of motion (with a visually matched dot array control); valid trials were those on which infants kept valid eye tracking data for at least 50% of a 2-s stimulus presentation. There was 91.8% valid data.

Upright walkers (M = 61.7%, 95% CI [59.2, 64.2]) received significantly more of infant’s total looking time than the paired control, t(63) = 5.84, p < .001, d = 0.73; they were first looked at on 68% of trials (significantly greater than chance, χ2(1) = 13.76, p < .001). In contrast, inverted walkers (M = 51.9%) were not looked at significantly greater than chance, t(63) = 1.21, p = .23, nor was the scrambled control display (M = 49.8%), t(63) = −0.18, p = .86. When infant age, sex, trial type and trial order were entered as fixed effects in a linear mixed effects model, there was a significant main effect of display type, F(2, 126) = 12.47, p < .001. Post-hoc tests revealed that upright walkers (mean difference = 9.8 percentage points, p = .002 relative to inverted walkers; mean difference = 11.9 percentage points, p < .001 relative to the scrambled control) were looked at significantly more than the other two displays. The effect of display type was neither significantly moderated by infant age nor sex. By 5–7 months, infants seem to be able to detect the coherent kinematic properties of human biological motion and not just local movement of the dots or overall stimulus energy.

paper_section_15_glm.text:
Abstract
Mindfulness training has been suggested as a cost-effective strategy to improve working memory capacity (WMC), although individual studies show inconsistent and variable effects. The aim of this meta-analysis is to estimate the overall effect of mindfulness-based interventions on WMC and identify moderators of the effectiveness of such training. Following a search of PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus for articles from January 2000 to March 2024, 38 eligible studies (k = 41 independent samples; N = 3,247 participants) were included that contrasted mindfulness training with active or no intervention controls and measured WMC with behavioral tasks (e.g., complex span tasks, n-back tasks, Operation Span task). The random-effects model produced a small-to-moderate overall effect (Hedges's g = 0.38, 95% CI [0.24, 0.52], p < .001) with substantial heterogeneity (Q = 96.4, I 2 = 58.6%). The moderator analysis showed a greater effect for longer interventions (≥ 8 weeks vs. < 8 weeks, β = 0.21, p = .012) as well as for interventions administered by an instructor (vs. an app, g = 0.46 vs. 0.22, p = .031) on samples with a higher initial stress (e.g., students during exams and military personnel before deployment). Effects were not significantly affected by age range, type of meditation (focus vs. open monitoring), and publication year. The Risk-of-Bias assessment (RoB 2) led to the categorization of 12, 21, and 5 studies as low, some concerns, and high risk, respectively, while Egger's regression test revealed a possible presence of small study effect (p = .048), and the trim and fill analysis produced a corrected negative estimate (g = 0.31). The sensitivity analyses showed the robustness of the overall effect against outlier and control conditions. Overall, this review suggests that structured mindfulness training (particularly if it is at least 8 weeks and led by an instructor) can produce modest but stable improvements in working memory capacity. The results must be interpreted in light of the observed heterogeneity and possible publication bias. We discuss the implications for cognitive training research and propose recommendations for future randomized trials (e.g., preregistration, proper active control, and higher sample size).

Keywords: mindfulness, working memory, meta-analysis, cognitive training, intervention.

Abstract
Training mindfulness has been suggested as a low-cost approach to improve working memory capacity (WMC), but individual studies show inconsistent and sometimes small training effects. Here, we performed a meta-analysis to determine the net effect of mindfulness-based interventions on WMC, and to examine factors that moderate the effectiveness of such interventions. In a literature search (PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus) covering the period January 2000 to March 2024, we selected 38 studies (k = 41 independent samples, N = 3,247) that compared the effects of mindfulness-training vs. active or no control interventions on WMC (e.g., as measured by complex span tasks, n-back tasks, and the Operation Span task). A random effects model showed small-to-moderate net effects of training on WMC (Hedges's g = 0.38, 95% CI [0.24, 0.52], p < .001), accompanied by substantial between-study heterogeneity (Q = 96.4, I2 = 58.6%). In moderator tests, we found larger effect sizes for longer training duration (≥ 8 weeks vs. < 8 weeks; β = 0.21, p = .012), for live (as opposed to app-based) training (g = 0.46 vs. 0.22, p = .031), and for participants in highly stressed situations (e.g., students during exams and military personnel before deployment). Effects were not significantly moderated by age group, meditation approach (focused attention vs. open monitoring), or publication year. According to the RoB 2 test, 12 studies had a low risk of bias, 21 had some concerns, and 5 had a high risk of bias. Egger's regression test suggested a potential for small-study effects (p = .048), and the trim-and-fill method lowered the adjusted effect size to g = 0.31. Sensitivity analyses showed that the overall effect size was stable with regard to the presence of outliers and type of control intervention. Our findings indicate that formal mindfulness training-especially if lasting 8 weeks or longer and led by a live instructor-may have small but consistent effects on WMC. These effects should be considered in light of the between-study heterogeneity and likely small-study effects. We discuss the implications for the field of cognitive training, and provide recommendations for future randomized controlled trials (e.g., preregistration, robust active control groups, larger sample sizes).

Keywords: mindfulness, working memory, meta-analysis, cognitive training, intervention

paper_section_17_sonnet.text:
Methods
To estimate the employment impacts of the 2014 Seattle minimum wage ordinance, we employ a difference-in-differences analysis relative to a synthetic control group (combining nearby King County ZIP codes and similar labor markets in Washington State outside of the Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue metropolitan statistical area). The Seattle minimum wage ordinance passed by the Seattle City Council on June 2, 2014, increases the city's minimum wage gradually, starting April 1, 2015, from the state minimum of $9.47 to $11.00 initially (for large firms, 500+ employees) and up to $15.00 by January 1, 2017 (large firms without medical benefits) and by January 1, 2019 (small firms).

Our main data are quarterly Unemployment Insurance (UI) wage data from the Washington State Employment Security Department from 2005Q1-2018Q4. We focus on hourly workers in food service (NAICS 722) and retail trade (NAICS 44-45), which are industries that employ a disproportionate share of minimum wage bound workers. We create a balanced panel of 2,847 establishments with complete data for the full sample period and pair them with comparison groups using propensity score weights with pre-treatment (2005Q1-2014Q2) trends in hours, headcount, and average hourly wages.

Our baseline model is specified as follows: Y i,t=βSeattle i Post t +α i +γ t +X i,t δ +ε i,t where Y i,t is employment or hours (log) for establishment i in quarter t. Seattle i is a dummy for treated establishments. Post t is a dummy for quarters after April 2015. α i and γ t are establishment and quarter fixed effects. X i,t also includes establishment size and single-site status. All standard errors are clustered by ZIP code (94 clusters). We test for parallel trends using coefficients from an event study regression, with separate coefficients for each quarter from 2013Q1 to 2018Q4, omitting 2015Q1 as the baseline period. We also present results disaggregated by wage bins ($9.47-$11, $11-$13, and > $13) to estimate heterogeneous wage "bite" of the policy.

Methods
We apply a difference-in-differences method to estimate the employment impact of the 2014 Seattle minimum wage ordinance by comparing Seattle to a synthetic control, based on a weighted combination of surrounding King County ZIP codes and other similar labor markets across Washington State (but outside the Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue metropolitan statistical area). The Seattle City Council approved the ordinance (June 2, 2014) to increase the minimum wage in increments, starting April 1, 2015, from the state minimum of $9.47 to $11.00 (large employers, 500+), $15.00 by Jan 1, 2017 (large employers no medical) and by Jan 1, 2019 (small employers).

Our main data source is the quarterly Unemployment Insurance (UI) wage data from the Washington State Employment Security Department, 2005Q1-2018Q4, which we limit to hourly jobs in food service (NAICS 722) and retail trade (NAICS 44-45), the two industries with the largest shares of minimum wage bound jobs. We create a balanced panel of 2,847 establishments followed every period, which we match to other establishments based on propensity score weighting of pre-period (2005Q1-2014Q2) trends in hours, headcount, and average hourly wage.

We estimate: Y_it = β(Seattle_i × Post_t) + α_i + γ_t + X_it'δ + ε_it Where Y_it is log employment or log hours for establishment i in quarter t. Seattle_i is a dummy for treated establishments, Post_t is dummy for quarters after April 2015, α_i and γ_t are establishment and quarter dummies, and X_it includes establishment size and single site dummies. We use ZIP code (94 clusters) clustered standard errors. We test parallel trends assumptions by estimating event study coefficients for each quarter (2013Q1-2018Q4) separately (with 2015Q1 the omitted reference). We show results separately for wage tier bins ($9.47-$11, $11-$13, >$13) to assess heterogeneous bite of the minimum wage at different points in the wage distribution.

The unusual $T_g$ behavior of PMMA/PVDF blends is related to a large mismatch in their segmental dynamics: the typical $T_g$ for PMMA is around 105--125$\degree$C while PVDF has a $T_g$ around $-$50$\degree$C. Still, DSC is often able to find only a single composition-dependent transition (not two separate glass transitions), indicating strong molecular level mixing, driven mainly by carbonyl groups of PMMA and the hydrogen-containing parts of PVDF. In particular, early DSC studies (Roerdink et al., 1978) found compatibility in a wide range of compositions for isotactic, atactic and syndiotactic PMMA/PVDF blends. Still, $T_g$ did not obey a simple universal linear interpolation but rather was described by a Gordon-Taylor relation with composition- and tacticity-dependent $k$ factors of 2.38, 1.72 and 1.39 for isotactic, atactic and syndiotactic PMMA, respectively (Roerdink et al., 1978[\href{https://doi.org/10.1016/0032-3861(78)90034-4}{DoI:10.1016/0032-3861(78)90034-4}](https://doi.org/10.1016/0032-3861(78)90034-4)).

In particular at high PVDF concentrations, this "paradox" can be affected by crystallization, nanoscale concentration fluctuations resulting in broadened or shifted $T_g$. Indeed Huang and Zhang (2004) found indications of weak specific interactions (e.g. in the IR spectra of carbonyl stretching shifts), but at the same time found that at high PVDF fractions, the blends became more heterogeneous and opaque. A single $T_g$ in the DSC, therefore, does not necessarily imply complete thermodynamic homogeneity. In 2020, for 4:1 and 3:2 PMMA/PVDF blends, dielectric relaxation studies indicated an increase in relaxation amplitude and conductivity suggesting the presence of compositional inhomogeneity on the nanoscale (Gonçalves et al., 2020[\href{https://doi.org/10.1080/00222348.2020.1847393}{DoI:10.1080/00222348.2020.1847393}](https://doi.org/10.1080/00222348.2020.1847393)). The surprising $T_g$ behavior, therefore, can be explained as a competition between specific interchain interactions, composition dependent free volume, crystallinity of PVDF and processing factors. Ultimately, therefore, a more thorough interpretation requires the simultaneous use of DSC, spectroscopy, DMA and dielectric data, not just of $T_g$ as a tool to judge binary miscibility.

The anomalous glass transition of PMMA/PVDF blends arises due to the major discrepancy in the segmental dynamics as PMMA commonly show Tg values in the range of 105-125 C, while PVDF shows a Tg around −50 C. The differential scanning calorimetry often shows that instead of two separate glass transitions, a composition dependent single transition is often observed, suggesting strong molecular level miscibility largely due to the interaction between carbonyl groups of PMMA and hydrogen bearing groups of PVDF. It was shown in early calorimetry studies by Roerdink et al. (1978) that PMMA/PVDF blends (iso, atactic, and syndiotactic) show compatibility over wide ranges of compositions. However, the Tg's were not found to be following any universal linear interpolation. Instead the Tg's were found to be fitted to the Gordon-Taylor relation with composition (and tacticity) dependent k values (2.38, 1.72, and 1.39) for isotactic, atactic, and syndiotactic PMMA respectively ([Roerdink et al., 1978](https://doi.org/10.1016/0032-3861(78)90034-4)).

At high PVDF contents, the anomaly can be more evident as crystallization and nanoscale composition fluctuations can cause broadening and/or shifts. Huang and Zhang (2004) found evidence of weak specific interactions (e.g. shift in the infrared carbonyl stretching), but also increasing heterogeneity and opacity with rising PVDF content. So the detection of a single transition by DSC alone should not suggest complete thermodynamic homogeneity. Indeed in 2020 dielectric relaxation studies of 4:1 and 3:2 PMMA/PVDF blends showed higher relaxation strength and conductivity due to compositional heterogeneity on the nanoscale ([Gonçalves et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1080/00222348.2020.1847393)). The intriguing glass transition behaviour can be attributed to the interplay of specific interchain interactions, composition-dependent free volume, PVDF crystallinity and processing history. For an accurate analysis of such systems, in addition to DSC studies, spectroscopy, DM and dielectric studies should be performed and Tg shouldn't be used as the only parameter to judge the binary miscibility.

Introduction One of the most critical but poorly optimized decisions in cancer care is the dose of chemotherapy. Current SOC dosing of cytotoxic chemotherapy agents (eg, 5-fluorouracil, carboplatin, doxorubicin) was largely defined by population dose finding studies of the 1980s/90s in many cases set as constant body surface area normalized doses with mandated dose-modifications for toxicity. This "cookie-cutter" approach fails to account for significant inter and intra-patient pharmacokinetic heterogeneity (often >10-fold variation in drug clearance) that characterizes cytotoxic chemotherapy. This has predictable clinical implications for under-treatment leading to poor tumor control vs. over-treatment leading to grade 3-4 neutropenia, neuropathy and treatment discontinuation. For example, in mCRC FOLFOX administration, retrospective analysis has indicated that in fewer than 30% of cases was the dose administered what post hoc modeling implies to have been the optimal (well tolerated) dose trajectory.

Dose management is an optimal control problem well suited to the framework of reinforcement learning (RL). Chemotherapy dosing can be cast as an ideal Markov decision process, where a clinician (agent) receives a state (blood counts, grades of toxicity, biomarkers, performance status) at each treatment cycle and chooses an action (dose level, time, drug alteration) and receives a reward based on the trade-off between tumor response and cumulative toxicity. Proof of concept studies by Zhao et al. (2011) showed a (fully observable) RL agent learning on simulated patient data could do better than fixed approaches in a compartmental model of myelosuppression. Recent years have seen the application of offline RL algorithms (conservative Q-learning, policy constraint via behavior cloning and doubly robust off-policy evaluation) to leverage observational EMR data for learning without high-risk on-policy exploration in vulnerable patients. The 2022-2024 TempoRL and related dose optimization efforts at institutions such as MD Anderson and Duke are starting to bring these tools to bear on prospective assessment.

However, there are many hurdles between retrospective RL benchmarks and deployable trial interventions. These range from partial observability of disease burden, patient non-stationarity across treatment courses, risk-averse policy constraints, and regulatory uncertainties (eg, FDA guidance on adaptive trial design and AI/ML based software as medical device). In this paper we will summarize adaptive chemotherapy dosing as an RL problem, assess methodological advantages/disadvantages of published work and propose a trial design (off-policy confidence bounds, clinician in the loop with policy veto) as necessary for first-in-human evaluation.

Introduction

Optimal chemotherapy dosing is among the most critical and under-optimized decisions in oncology. Most current standard of care dosing for cytotoxic drugs (5-fluorouracil, carboplatin, doxorubicin, etc) was defined by population-based dose-finding studies from the 1980s-90s that typically used a body surface area-normalized fixed dosing and toxicity-driven, protocol-defined dose reductions. These fixed dose schemes fail to account for large (often >10-fold) inter/intra-individual variability in pharmacokinetic parameters such as drug clearance, which is common in cytotoxic chemotherapy. As a result, both under-and over-dosing are well-recognized in clinical practice (resulting in poor tumor control vs. grade 3/4 neutropenia, neuropathy, and treatment discontinuation respectively). For example, in metastatic colorectal cancer retrospective studies of FOLFOX administration demonstrate that <30% of patients appear to have received the post hoc optimal dose trajectory by dose modeling.

Chemotherapy dosing is a quintessentially sequential decision problem amenable to solution with reinforcement learning (RL). It can be modeled as a straightforward Markov decision process where the clinician observes a patient state (blood counts, toxicity grades, biomarkers, performance status) each treatment cycle, takes an action (e.g., dose level/timing, or change in drug) and gets a reward representing tumor response vs. cumulative toxicity. Initial proof-of-concept studies (Zhao et al, 2011) have shown that a fully observable RL agent trained on synthetic patient data could do better than fixed protocols in a model of myelosuppression based on compartmental dynamics. Recently, approaches to offline RL (conservative Q-learning, behavior-clone policy constraints, doubly robust off-policy evaluation) have made it possible to learn from electronic health record data in observational settings without risk of dangerous exploration in vulnerable populations. Recent efforts (2022-24TempoRL, etc.) at institutions such as MD Anderson and Duke to adapt these approaches for prospective evaluation are underway.

However, there remain major gaps between retrospective benchmarks with RL and practical trial implementation such as partial observability of disease burden, non-stationarity of patient physiology across treatment courses, strong safety constraints, and regulatory challenges in FDA adaptive trial guidance and use of AI/ML for software as a medical device. In this paper, we describe the formulation of adaptive chemotherapy dosing as an RL problem, summarize the strengths and limitations of existing published approaches for RL, and describe a trial design (using off-policy confidence bounds and clinician-in-the-loop policy veto) that we believe is a necessary step towards first-in-human testing.

Got laid off from teaching in August... 
 Here's what I learned in my first 60 days 
 On Aug 12 (2 days before inservice week began) I received a call from my principal at Jefferson Elementary that my position was being "eliminated by declining enrollment." Six years as a 4th grade teacher. Over in four minutes on the phone. 
 I'm not looking for sympathy, I'm writing this because the past couple months have been a crazy education of their own and I wish someone had told me these things day 1. 
 - Getting unemployed paperwork is a JOB. It took 3 weeks and 2 rejections of my paperwork before I realized I entered in the date of my last day of work wrong. File asap and check and double check. It wasn't until Sept 19th that I got my first check. 
 - Your teaching skills are useful in many more ways than you think, but nobody knows that. I was applying for "training" and "instructional design" type jobs. Getting nowhere. I made changes to my resume to say "managed 28-person team, presented 6 hour presentations daily, analyzed performance data." Rather than "taught 4th grade." Within 2 weeks I've had 4 interviews. I'll start as a customer success rep for a software company in Cedar Rapids on Monday the 14th. It's not teaching. It's a $9k raise over the district. 
 - You will have weird grief. On August 20th I broke down crying in the school supply aisle at Target. Who saw that coming? Allow yourself these things. 
 - People want to help you. You just have to ask for it. A previous parent heard about my lay off and hooked me up with the company that I ended up working for. I never would have known about this job on indeed. 
 So for all the teachers still in the classroom who may be concerned about their job. You need to start updating your resume NOW. Not waiting on the phone call. 
 Feel free to ask me questions in comments. And to everyone at Jefferson... miss you guys.

June 2021: I become the de facto town beekeeper for my town by mistake. 
 One day there is a bee swarm on the maple outside my house in Cedar Falls. I contact the town, the fire department, 3 different pest control companies. All of them say, "Do not disturb them". I post a picture in the town Facebook group. Dennis, a retired beekeeper, shows up at my house with a cardboard box, a sheet, and the cool demeanor of a bomb disposal technician. 
 We trap most of the swarm in the box but there are hundreds of bees left. Dennis says they should probably disperse by morning. Nope. They nest in my porch ceiling. 
 For the next couple weeks people start messaging me. "There are bees in my chimney. Oak Street." "We've got some bees in our mailbox. Franklin Avenue." "I saw some bees hanging from a playground fence. Lincoln Elementary." Everyone seems to think I'm an expert. 
 Well, I'm not an expert. I've watched 4 videos on Youtube or something. 
 I buy a veil. I borrow Dennis's smoker. I start contacting actual beekeepers. By August I've helped organize removing 11 swarms (one off the town library ceiling!). The librarian sent me a thank you card with the whole staff's signatures. My 7yo daughter calls me the "bee lady" (I'm a dude named Mark). 
 Then, weirdly, people keep calling me! Last month I get a voicemail. "Suspicious buzzing around the courthouse!" 
 I'm no beekeeper. I don't own a beehive or anything. I just picked up a phone in 2021.

1 year / 15,000 miles on my 2023 Model Y (honest review and $600 bullshit) 
 Got my Model Y Long Range in Costa Mesa, CA delivery center in March 2023. I thought it was a good time for an honest review (and not a honeymoon phase one) at the 1-year mark. 
 Pros: Still enjoying the hell out of the acceleration every day.  Coming from a 2018 Honda CR-V - this is mind boggling.  I pay ~$11 to charge at home (on a 240v plug).  Paid $70+ at the gas station.  Supercharger network is great.  Went to Phoenix in Jan and never worried about range.  I love having AP (autopilot) on 5 freeway when traffic is crazy. 
 Cons: Still see panel gaps on my rear driver door.  Wipers still seem to be guessing sometimes.  Sentry mode seems to drain the battery pretty noticeably.  Blind spot indicator is physical? Come on!!!  This is a big complaint from me.  (Had some phantom braking thing happen twice when driving on I10.  Scary shit twice.) 
 $600 repair story: Touchscreen in November started random rebooting when driving.  I went to the Costa Mesa service center, they had it for 4 days.  They told me it was a bad MCU4 connector.  Is it covered?  No.  Because I had a 3rd party aftermarket dash cam installed in Sept, they said there was voltage interference.  $612 later.  Is it valid?  Is it a bullshit?  I'll never know. 
 Final Verdict: 8/10.  Driving experience is worth it.  Savings are there.  Quality and service accountability keeps it from being higher.  Would I buy again?  Maybe.  Probably.  But maybe not the aftermarket electronics. 
 Ask me questions in the comments if you want.

Field Research Log - Bird Population Counts - Cedar Swamp
Week of May 6 - 15, 2024
Submitted by: Dana Whitfield, Field Technician, Northline Audubon Society

Summary of Activity:
Our 3 person team (D. Whitfield, M. Okafor, intern J. Reyes) conducted 40 point counts (covering all 8 existing points) over 10 straight days at the Cedar Swamp monitoring grid, both mornings (0530 - 0900) and evenings (1700 - 1930). We had good weather for most counts except for the May 9 morning count when we were forced to stop counting due to heavy rain.

Results:
We identified a total of 42 species (vs 37 same time last year) with a total of 1184 individual detections. Notable/highlights:
Virginia rail detected 4 times at station 3 - possibly breeding pair (last confirmed 2019)
Prothonotary warbler - 1 male singing at station 6 on May 11, 13; flagged for nest box checkup
Great Blue Heron active rookery near the north dike with at least 6 nests active
Swamp sparrow and Common yellowthroat continue to be the dominant species, representing about 22% of all detections

Stations 3 and 6 had 38% of total detections, likely due to the increase in emergent marsh habitat from last fall's hydrology restoration effort.

We have entered all data in eBird and our internal Northline database. Still need to review the audio recordings from the autonomous recording units (ARU) at stations 2 & 7 - J. Reyes will review by May 22.

Issues/Recommendations:
1. The boardwalk from station 4 to 5 is falling apart with two loose planks. Recommend maintenance prior to our June survey period.
2. High mosquito population this year - teams should bring mosquito repellent to carry through the rest of the spring counts.

FIELD RESEARCH LOG - BIRD POPULATION COUNTS CEDAR SWAMP
Week May 6 - 15, 2024
Submitted By: Dana Whitfield - Field Technician Northline Audubon Society

SUMMARY OF ACTIVITY
3 - person team (D. Whitfield, M. Okafor and intern J. Reyes) executed 40 point count surveys on Cedar Swamp monitoring grid for 10 straight days. All 8 established survey stations were sampled in morning (0530 - 0900) and evening (1700 - 1930). Weather was favorable, except May 9 morning survey was shortened due to heavy rains.

RESULTS
42 species recorded vs. 37 for the same time period last year. 1184 individual count: Highlights and notable:
- Virginia rail - detected at station 3 4x. Could be breeding pair? Last detected in 2019.
- Prothonotary warbler - 1 male singing at station 6 (May 11 and 13). See note below for nest box follow up evaluation.
- Great blue heron - active rookery near north dike. At least 6 nests occupied.
- Swamp sparrow and common yellowthroat still dominate the counts. 22% of overall detections.

Stations 3 and 6 produce 38% of overall detections.
Station abundance variability exists. Possibly due to last fall hydrology restoration that has increased emergent marsh area.
Data in eBird and our internal Northline database is now complete. Audio of autonomous recording unit (ARU) at Stations 2 and 7 not yet reviewed.
J. Reyes will complete by May 22nd.

ISSUES / RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Boardwalk between 4 and 5 deteriorating. Two planks are loose. Recommend repair before June survey round.
2. Mosquitoes are bad this season. Teams should bring mosquito spray for remainder of spring surveys.
3. Based upon prothonotary warbler detection, we recommend installation of two nest boxes near Station 6. Prior to June 1.

My sister and I went to Trattoria Roma on a rainy Friday evening (3/14/19) around 7:30pm after a Cubs game. We were told to expect a 25 minute wait but were seated within 15 minutes. For a Friday, awesome! Its a small place with exposed brick, dim lighting, a little loud but in a good way not in the "you can't talk to one another" way. 
 Now why am I writing this? - THE CARBONARA. This dish is going to cost you $19.95 which is on the money for the area. But here is the thing... this was a way better than you would expect. The pasta was home made and you could tell by the texture. It was cooked slightly past al dente which some might not approve but it was good. The sauce was nice and smooth... No cream was used at all. Just egg yolk, pecorino and all that amazing guanciale grease. The pork was cut into larger chunks with crispy edges. Not those sad little bits of bacon you see in other places. It all came together with some good hearty black pepper. Oh it was a good size portion. I could not eat it all. And I don't say that often. 
 Our server was great. He didn't hover but was attentive. Our server was Daniela and she came over when she should and made sure we were always filled up with water. There was also a bread basket with a herbed olive oil dip that we killed while we waited. 
 The house Chianti ($9 glass) could have been a little fuller and we had to prop up our table by putting a folded napkin under one of the legs (thanks Daniela) 
 Street parking in this area can be bad. Pay for valet. 
 Two people with shared tiramisu (oh my was it good. With a punch of real espresso) and drinks. It was $78 before tip. Its worth it. I will be back to get the cacio e pepe!

review_product_05_luna.text:
In Matt Haig’s novel The Midnight Library, Nora Seed, a 35-year old in Bedford, is living on the border of life and death after trying to take her own life. Within the strange library, where her former school librarian Mrs Elm leads her, Nora is able to check out different lives by opening books that reflect the paths her life could have taken – maybe she could have been an Olympic swimmer, maybe she could have owned a pub in Australia, or maybe she could have married Dan, or been a glaciologist.

The concept is enticing from the start, and Haig’s portrayal of Nora’s depression is sympathetic and relatable. I enjoyed the core concept of the library, that our regrets make us think there is a single decision that could have resolved everything, but that all lives have their own difficulties. The chapters are short and very readable. The details of swimming, music, chess and the Arctic are intriguing and help evoke the vivid possibilities of Nora’s life, like a dream.

At times the novel seems to spell out what it has to say. Nora’s epiphanies don’t always feel like insights she learns, but more like inspirational quotes. I was also a bit let down by the conclusion. It’s a positive one, and I can see why Haig wanted to give Nora hope – a sense of potential, but I thought it was a bit hurried and neat after all the emotional darkness of the start. There is barely any transition back to Nora’s original life, and this smooths out some of the complexities in her mental health challenges, reducing them to a simple message about the value of choosing to live.

It’s still a sympathetic and creative book that is quite easy to get caught up in emotionally. I didn’t always feel like the philosophical themes were subtle, but I did reflect on Nora’s journey. Particularly the message that there might be more potential in even an average life than we appreciate.

The Midnight Library by Matt Haig
35 year old Nora Seed, living in Bedford, tries to commit suicide, and ends up hovering between life and death. She finds herself in a strange library where, under the guidance of Mrs Elm (her old school librarian), she is able to check out books on various lives she could have led. She could be an Olympic swimmer, or own a pub in Australia, or be married to Dan, or study glaciology.

It’s a wonderfully intriguing concept, and Haig does an admirable job of dealing with the subject of depression - he makes it easy to relate to Nora. I particularly enjoyed the concept of the library - the idea that our regrets lead us to think that if we’d just made the right decision once, everything would have been okay, but the thing is, there are always going to be complications in life. The chapters are short and easy to read, the details about swimming, and music, and chess, and the Arctic give life to Nora’s various options, and make them seem kind of dreamy.

But at times the book is a little heavy-handed in trying to convey its message. It feels like Nora’s insights are more like inspiring quotes than real insights gained from living. I was slightly let down by the conclusion. It’s an optimistic one, and I suppose Haig wants to give Nora some sense of possibility, but it seems a little hurried and tidy after the gloomy mood at the start. Nora’s return to her current life is so swift that the more complicated issues with her mental health are somehow simplified to a lesson about deciding to live.

But this is a kind and imaginative book, with a strong emotional appeal. I didn’t always find all the philosophy subtle, but I thought about Nora’s journey, and in particular how she makes me realise how many possibilities there can be in a regular life.

Just finished a 3,000 mile trip from Portland to San Diego and back in my 2022 RAV4 Hybrid.  Kicking myself for taking the time to write this. 
 39.8 MPG on the entire trip.  Calculated manually from 9 fill ups.  (For those wondering, the computer shows about 1mpg higher than actual.)  EPA on this vehicle says 40 mpg combined.  In the flat-ish Central Valley when just cruising on the highway, I consistently got 42-43 mpg (at 70mph).  On mountain roads by Grant's Pass and the Grapevine, it dropped to about 34 mpg, but that's to be expected. 
 The 2.5 hybrid isn't too bad - although not terribly exciting.  Onramps onto I-5 take some strategy.  219 hp is ok, but not particularly enthusiastic and the CVT makes a lot of drone if you pin it.  But this isn't a sports car.  I was pleasantly surprised with comfort level.  After 500 mile days my back (and my wife's) held up well.  Good seats, reasonable road noise (much less than the RAV4 gasoline (gas) only vehicle I test drove in 2021), and ample space in the back for 2 duffels, a cooler, and a dog crate. 
 The infotainment display seems a generation behind.  The lane assist (XLE trim) is pretty annoying on curvy Hwy 101 and ends up getting turned off all the time.  Also, the brakes seem to have a "grabby" feeling at the beginning.  All Toyota hybrids have this but takes a couple hundred miles to adjust to. 
 Approximately 75 gallons of fuel used on the trip.  Approx. $340 at CA/OR fuel prices.  This would have been almost twice the cost for a comparable gas SUV. 
 Would I do it again?  Yes.  If you want something for road trips that doesn't use much fuel, that can carry some load, and only require oil changes this is a pretty good option.

Got the Logitech M240 Silent ($24.99 at Best Buy (bought Sept 2)) to replace my MX Anywhere 3 ($79.99) which I've been using every day for the last 2 years. It's been 3 weeks. For most people don't bother with the extra $55. 
 
 M240 only connects via bluetooth. No logi bolt receiver. Took like 4 seconds to connect to my M2 macbook air.  It has the standard "clicky" mouse scroll wheel. No MX free spinning hyper scroll wheel. So browsing a 2000 row excel sheet will take way longer.  2 side buttons. Same as the MX. Both can be easily remapped in logi options +. Sensor has 4000 dpi (MX anywhere 3 has 8000). I didn't really notice on desk but when using my lap and knee as a mousepad I noticed occasional jumping. 
 
 But the m240 is better at battery life. Logitech claims 18 months on 1x AA. After 1 month battery app still saying 100%. MX needs usb-c charged every 2-3 months with normal use. It's also 15g lighter (78g vs 99g) which can make a difference when you're carrying it around to cafes like I do every day. 
 
 Feels cheaper/more hollow sounding clicks. There's also a visible seam on the bottom. But actual clicks are quieter which is nice for when I'm on calls. 
 
 If you're just going to use it with 1 computer and don't really need multi device switching (MX Anywhere 3 does 3 devices with logi bolt or bluetooth and just a button press) then m240 is like 90% of what you're going to use every day for 1/3 of the cost. I'll stick to my mx for desk setup and m240 for traveling.

I'm normally not a fan of roguelike games. I find the need to do the same levels over and over again after death is much more annoying than enjoyable. 
 However, *Hades* is an exception to that. I began playing on Nintendo Switch in March 2024, expecting to give up after a couple of tries. But, I wound up playing for about 35 hours attempting to break free from the Underworld as Zagreus. 
 The gameplay is quick yet very simple: you dash, swing, cast, and try out a new assortment of boons for every run. What made the game the most enjoyable for me was picking upgrades from Athena, Artemis, and Dionysus and watching a normal sword become quite something. I usually discovered a new weapon, dialogue, ability, or even a story if I died in Tartarus or Elysium, so it was never a total loss to return to the House of Hades. 
 The most astonishing thing is the characters in the game. Zagreus, Hades, Nyx, Achilles, Megaera... all have great personalities. There's always new dialogue to go through. The voice acting and soundtrack really help it not feel like you're just grinding in this game when you go through everything so many times. It makes it feel like you're on a journey. 
 On Switch, it's playable on handheld with no issues. Every attempt to break free from the Underworld is easily played in 20-40 minute chunks. Some late game bouts got pretty hectic to do on a smaller screen, but I never really had any major issues. 
 I don't really consider myself a fan of roguelike games, but *Hades* is so approachable and cool looking and just gives so much that even casual gamers can enjoy. It's one of my favorite games on my Switch.

1/ I closed my first startup, [RelayCart](relaycart.com), in Nov 2021 after 18 months. We raised $120K, got 47 paying customers and still couldn't turn a profit.

2/ Lesson 1: There is a big difference between important and urgent. The small business owners liked our inventory dashboard, but they weren't ready to shake up their habits (and pay for it)

3/ Lesson 2: The only exponential validation is revenue. Words of encouragement, the waitlist, all the "definitely would use" comments...they don't pay the bills.

4/ Lesson 3: We scaled too quickly. By March 2021 we had a team of 4 burning $14k/month before finding product-market fit.

5/ Lesson 4: Interview your users weekly. I was too often in Oakland hacking away and not enough in the shops we said we were helping

6/ Lesson 5: Make sure you're on the same page with your cofounder. My co-founder was ready to start raising money. I was focused on profitability. We let the difference simmer too long.

7/ Lesson 6: Have kill thresholds. We should have killed it when we were at <$5k MRR for 6 months. Instead we let it die when our bank account reached $8300.

8/ Lesson 7: If you learn from failure it's a really expensive lesson. Now I'm coding slower. Selling sooner. Testing actions, not intentions.

1/ I closed my first startup RelayCart after 18 months in Nov '21. We raised $120k, grew to 47 paying users. Still couldn't sustain.

2/ #1 Sometimes problems are real, but not urgent. Small retailers loved our inventory dashboard, but few were ready to shift habits or pay for it.

3/ #2 Only revenue doubles down. While we got lots of love, waitlists, "I'd totally use this!" not enough revenue to pay salaries.

4/ #3 Don't hire too fast. Our team of 4 was on $14k/month burn by March '21 w/o product-market fit.

5/ #4 Speak to customers weekly. Too much time in Oakland building and not enough in front of the store owners we said we were building for.

6/ #5 Alignment with your co-founder is critical. My co-founder wanted to raise, I wanted to go profitable. We let that fester until we couldn't ignore it.

7/ #6 Set kill thresholds. We should have closed after 6 months at <$5k MRR. Not when we got down to $8.3k bank balance.

8/ #7 Failures are costly degrees. But only if you take them. I'm now building less, selling more and measuring behavior vs enthusiasm.

social_post_03_glm.text:
Just wrapped hiring 12 junior devs at Shopify. 
Here's what actually caught my attention looking through 400+ resumes. 
Thread? 
Nah. Just some real shit. 
1) solving problems - 
I don't care about your Netflix clone. 
But one person made a schedule app for her dentist mom's Mississauga clinic. 
With auth, DB, real users? 
Forget the todo lists, people. 
2) Showing growth - 
A 3 month bootcamp certificate is less interesting than a github history of you consistently pushing code over 12+ months (even on small projects). 
Consistent > Intense 
3) Respecting my time - 
Brevity was king. 
Having bullet points that showed what you made and how and the impact ("got page load time down from 4s to 1.2s"). 
I only needed 1 page max (you guys are junior, come on). 
4) Showing curiosity - 
Blog posts, Stack overflow answers, or even just a curious question in a PR description. 
Actually ended up hiring two people from amazing code review comments on open source repos. 
5) What I didn't care about. 
- Fancy schools (5/12 were self-taught) 
- Length of cover letter (single para was fine) 
- Not knowing our exact stack 
(We teach Rails in-house week 1). 
Surprisingly, only 9/400 resumes talked about accessibility / testing. 
If you're a junior dev want the 2024 edge? 
Start there. 
For the 12 of you that joined us in Jan, welcome aboard! 
Everyone else - 
Keep building, keep deploying. 
Next cohort opening this fall. 
👀

Just hired 12 junior devs at Shopify. Here's what really caught my attention out of 400+ resumes.

A thread? Nah. Just some thoughts.

1/ Projects that actually solved problems. Sorry, no need for your Netflix clone. One candidate built a scheduling system for her mom's dental office in Mississauga. Auth? Check. DB? Check. Users? Check. Smashes every todo app on stackoverflow.

2/ Indicators you learn quickly. 3 month boot camp cert? Not as valuable as someone's Github activity where you can see consistent commit activity over 12+ months on maybe small projects. Consistent > intense

3/ Resumes that save me time. Short resumes won. Bullet points of things you built, using what, results ("reduced page load time from 4s to 1.2s") etc. One page is fine. You're junior, we expect that.

4/ Any indication of curiosity. Blog posts. Stack overflow answers. A question in a PR description. Two hires directly from awesome open source repo code review comments.

5/ No big schools (5 of 12 are self taught), length of cover letter (one parg was ok), or knowledge of our exact stack. We'll teach you rails week one.

Most surprising: Only 9 out of 400 resumes talked about accessibility or testing. Juniors, if you want to stand out in 2024, hit these.

Congrats to 12 of you starting in Jan. Welcoming you on the team. Everyone else, keep building, ship away.

New cohort starting up this fall. 👀

social_post_07_luna.text:
1/3 I learned 5 tough lessons from cold emailing 200 VCs to raise seed in spring 2024.

My mistake #1: My generic pitch was the same for all. "Hey we're the future of collaboration." Didn't matter if you're a NY Fintech investor or a Boston Healthcare VC.

My mistake #2: I focused on features not traction. Our best validation was $18.4K MRR with 37% MoM in March. It was on slide #12.

2/3 My mistake #3: I emailed partners who never invest in seed. They managed $500M+ funds but cut their first checks at Series A. I should've looked at their website and recent deals before emailing.

My mistake #4: I said "15 min to connect" vs. "Would you consider leading a $1.5M seed for a B2B workflow tool with 37% MoM?" My clear ask.

3/3 My mistake #5: My follow-up was emotional and inconsistent. I followed up with 4 emails in 10 days to some VCs. No follow-up at all after the initial email for others. Here's how I ended up. 3 thoughtful follow-ups in 21 days. Each one with new data.

We raised in July 2024. My big lesson: cold email isn't only about volume. It's about being relevant. Having proof. And timing. Not sending 200 emails.

1/3 Cold emailed 200 VCs raising my seed round spring 2024 - here are 5 hard lessons learned

Mistake 1: Copy-pasted the same generic message to all of them. "Hey guys, we're doing the future of collaboration". Does not work for a NY fintech VC or a Boston healthcare VC.

Mistake 2: Focused on features, not traction. The best metric we had was MRR $18,400 & 37% MoM growth in March. And I buried that information on slide 12.

2/3 Mistake 3: Emailed partners that never touch the seed stage. A few had $500M+ funds but wrote their first checks only on Series A. Should have checked their website/latest deals before hitting send.

Mistake 4: Emailed to "get 15 mins to connect", instead of a clear specific request: "Would you be interested in leading $1.5M Seed for a B2B workflow tool 37% MoM growth?"

3/3 Mistake 5: Emotional, random follow-ups. For some VCs, I sent 4 emails in 10 days, for others 0 emails after the initial one. In the end: easy process was 3 thoughtful follow-ups in 21 days with a new data point.

July 2024 we closed our round. Learned: cold email is not just about sending numbers. It's about relevance, proof, and timing - not 200 emails.

social_post_15_glm.text:
After 19 years as a civil engineer, I quit at 43 to pursue a career as a data analyst.  Here's what I learned. 
 Mar 2023: After completing the city of Mesa's stormwater drainage project, an uncomfortable realization hit me.  The aspect of my job I enjoyed the most wasn't designing infrastructure, but creating the Excel models and dashboards that monitored our project budgets. 
 I decided to pursue a career change.  I spent 14 months studying on evenings and weekends: Google Data Analytics Certificate, followed by SQL (datacamp) and Python.  I completed 3 portfolio projects, including a 12-year analysis of Arizona rainfall data to forecast maintenance needs for drainage systems.  I integrated my previous domain expertise with my new skills. 
 May 2024: I got a job as a data analyst for a Phoenix logistics company.  I took a 12% salary reduction for the first year.  Now, 6 months later, I'm making more than when I was a senior civil engineer. 
 The one thing no one tells career changers: 
 1.  Your 'old' skills are an advantage, not a liability.  As an engineer, I found it easier to query and understand operational data than a bootcamp graduate with no real-world experience. 
 2.  Use your age as a weapon.  You have 20 years of experience communicating with stakeholders, managing timelines, and understanding how business works.  They can't teach that in a bootcamp. 
 3.  It's never too late... but it's also never cheap.  I sacrificed 14 months of weekends.  You pay the price. 
 If you're on the fence like I was for 3 years, this is your cue. 
 #CareerChange #DataAnalytics #CareerPivot #NeverTooLate

I quit my 19-year career as a civil engineer at 43 to become a data analyst. Here’s what I found out.

I finished the city of Mesa’s stormwater drainage project last March. And I had this realization that was hard to face. What I liked most about my work was not the infrastructure design, but creating the Excel models and dashboards to monitor our project budgets.

So I had to come up with a strategy. Google Data Analytics Certificate. Then SQL on DataCamp. Then Python. After 14 months of studying on nights and weekends, I did 3 portfolio projects. One to analyze 12 years of AZ rainfall to predict drainage maintenance schedules. I was able to use my old subject matter knowledge and the new skills.

And I got hired as a data analyst at a Phoenix-based logistics firm in May. 12% pay cut for the first year. And 6 months later, I make more money than when I was a senior civil engineer.

The thing nobody tells you about career changes.

1. Your “old” knowledge is valuable. I was better at querying and making sense of our operational data than a bootcamp guy without the subject matter experience.

2. Older is powerful. You’ve had 20 years of stakeholder interaction. Dealing with deadlines. Knowing how companies actually work? Not something they’ll learn at bootcamp.

3. It’s not too late. But it ain’t cheap either. I spent 14 months missing the weekends. That’s how much it costs.

So if you’re like I was for 3 years on the fence…here’s your sign.

#CareerChange #DataAnalytics #CareerPivot #NeverTooLate
